lessons.title: Allele and genotype frequencies from population samples
lessons.summary: Convert sampled genotypes into allele frequencies and connect genome variation to biological history.
objectives: Distinguish individuals, chromosomes, genotypes, alleles and sequence differences
Calculate and check diploid genotype and allele frequencies
Explain how sequencing, sample design and a null model connect a genomic pattern to a biological question
sections: Why natural populations are genetically different

Population genetics asks how much diversity a population contains, whether that diversity matches a model, and what history produced it. A population is a set of potentially interbreeding individuals, but the sampling boundary must be specified: a meadow, an island, an ancestry group or an entire species need not be the same statistical population. A locus is a genomic position or region; an allele is an alternative state at that locus; a diploid genotype contains two alleles. Evolution at a locus means allele frequencies change across generations, rather than simply that individuals differ.

The introductory slides use butterfly mimicry, closely related birds, hominin gene flow, reinforcement (selection strengthening reproductive isolation where costly hybridization occurs) between sympatric *Phlox*, and local adaptation in *Arabidopsis thaliana* to show that genomic differences can encode both demographic history and ecological function. Ancient-DNA methods associated with Svante Pääbo make past samples observable and allow comparisons with living populations. These cases motivate questions, not a rule that every variable site is adaptive.
From a sequenced genome to a testable pattern

Whole-genome sequencing reads many short DNA fragments, which must be mapped or assembled, quality checked and compared across samples. A read is not an independent chromosome: multiple reads may cover the same inherited gene copy. SNP calls summarize variation among chromosomes after filtering; missing data, sequencing errors and reference bias can change the inferred spectrum.

In the slide's *Arabis nemorensis* example, a demographic diagram proposes ancestral size around 150,000, descendant ancestral sizes around 25,000 and 59,000, and later sizes 6,000, 2,000, 6,000 and 14,000, with time labels near 900 and 10 thousand years. These are inferred model parameters, not direct censuses. The exchange arrows labeled “1/33 gen.” and “1/150 gen.” are retained here as source labels; their precise directional/rate convention needs instructor confirmation. Do not convert them into definitive migrant counts.

An alignment becomes summary statistics such as diversity, an SFS or differentiation. A null hypothesis $H_0$ predicts those summaries under specified mutation, drift, mating and demographic assumptions. Rejecting it supports a mismatch, not uniquely natural selection; $H_A$ may represent several biological or technical alternatives. This pattern-to-process distinction will recur in demographic and selection inference.
Counting gene copies: derivation and units

Let $N_{AA},N_{Aa},N_{aa}$ be numbers of sampled diploid individuals with the three genotypes. With $N=N_{AA}+N_{Aa}+N_{aa}$ individuals and $M=2N$ autosomal gene copies,



$$
f_{AA}=\frac{N_{AA}}N,\quad f_{Aa}=\frac{N_{Aa}}N,\quad f_{aa}=\frac{N_{aa}}N,
$$




$$
p=\frac{2N_{AA}+N_{Aa}}{2N}=f_{AA}+\frac12 f_{Aa},\qquad q=1-p.
$$



Each $AA$ supplies two $A$ copies and each $Aa$ one: this is why the allele-count denominator differs from the genotype-count denominator. Frequencies are dimensionless and sum to one within their respective sets. This calculation does not assume Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE); HWE is a later model predicting genotype frequencies from $p$. For a haploid sample, $M=N$; for other ploidies count the actual homologous copies. Do not infer diploid genotype counts from dominant phenotypes alone.
Sampling uncertainty and interpretation

If $M$ independent copies are sampled from a population with allele frequency $p$, the allele count $X$ is binomial, with $E[X]=Mp$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=Mp(1-p)$. Dividing by $M$ gives $\operatorname{Var}(\hat p)=p(1-p)/M$ and approximate standard error $\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/M}$. This is a sampling model, not yet drift across generations. Independent-copy assumptions may fail with related individuals, inbreeding, pooling demes or nonrandom collection; chromosome count alone then overstates precision. A sample frequency is an estimate, not the exact population value.

Always report sample location, sampling unit, ploidy, callable genotypes and missing-data exclusions alongside the frequency. The same count conversion prepares practical analyses of HWE, drift, selection and migration.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
variables: $N$: sampled diploid individuals; $M=2N$: autosomal gene copies
$N_{AA},N_{Aa},N_{aa}$: genotype counts; $f$: dimensionless genotype frequencies
$p,q$: frequencies of the arbitrarily named alleles $A,a$; $q$ need not be rarer
lessons.workedExample: Sample 80 individuals: 28 $AA$, 32 $Aa$, 20 $aa$. Then $N=80$, $M=160$; genotype frequencies are $0.35,0.40,0.25$. The $A$ count is $2(28)+32=88$, so $p=88/160=0.55$ and $q=0.45$. The check $0.35+0.5(0.40)=0.55$ agrees. Under an independent-copy sampling approximation, $\mathrm{SE}(\hat p)=\sqrt{0.55(0.45)/160}=0.0393$. This expresses precision, not the speed of evolutionary change. The observed heterozygote proportion is $0.40$; it has not been replaced by the HWE prediction $2pq=0.495$.

assessment.question: A sample has 28 AA, 32 Aa and 20 aa individuals. What is the A frequency?
Which denominator converts 32 heterozygotes among 80 individuals into an observed genotype frequency?
assessment.explanation: Genotype frequencies count individuals: 32/80=0.40.

assessment.question: What is the approximate standard error for p=0.55 among 160 independently sampled copies?
assessment.explanation: $\sqrt{0.55(0.45)/160}=0.0393$; 0.00155 is the variance, not its square root.

assessment.question: A sequencing dataset has 30 reads per individual. Which quantity describes chromosome sampling for a diploid autosomal locus?
assessment.explanation: Depth reduces genotype-call error; it does not multiply independent inherited copies.
options: Two inherited gene copies per callable individual

assessment.question: A neutral demographic model is rejected by a diversity statistic. Which conclusion is supported?
assessment.explanation: Rejection alone does not identify whether demography, selection or technical bias caused the departure.
options: At least one specified model or data assumption is inadequate

assessment.question: Only a dominant phenotype is measured. What is needed to count allele copies accurately?
assessment.explanation: AA and Aa can share a dominant phenotype; their copy contributions differ.
options: Genotypes or an explicitly justified inference model
Treat every dominant phenotype as AA
Assume p equals the phenotype frequency

assessment.question: The genotype-count formula for p requires HWE.
assessment.explanation: It is an accounting identity; HWE predicts genotype proportions and is not needed for counting.

assessment.question: The labels p and q can be assigned to either allele, even if q is common.
assessment.explanation: They designate states, not major/minor rank; always specify the label.

assessment.question: A sample frequency of 0.55 proves the population frequency is exactly 0.55.
assessment.explanation: Sampling error and design affect the estimate.

assessment.question: Under a biallelic model, genotype frequencies sum to one and p+q=1 are separate checks.
assessment.explanation: One check concerns individuals; the other concerns gene copies.

practice.question: For 10 AA, 20 Aa and 10 aa individuals, calculate both types of frequencies.
Why might 100 related individuals contain less information than 100 unrelated individuals?
practice.solution: Related gene copies share recent ancestry, violating independent sampling; uncertainty must account for family structure.

practice.question: Propose one demographic and one technical alternative to low diversity.
practice.solution: A bottleneck could reduce diversity; a strict missing-data or allele-frequency filter could remove real polymorphisms. Use sample metadata and callable-site denominators to distinguish them.

lessons.title: Quantifying molecular diversity
lessons.summary: Measure diversity using pairwise differences, segregating sites and frequency spectra while keeping sampling and polarization conventions explicit.
objectives: Calculate gene diversity, pi and Watterson theta on consistent locus/site scales
Construct folded, unfolded and joint spectra from allele counts
Explain singleton corrections, high-derived-frequency weighting and sequencing/polarization biases
sections: Diversity as a probability

A gene-diversity measure asks whether two randomly drawn copies differ. With population allele frequencies $p_j$, $H=1-\sum_j p_j^2$: subtract the probability of drawing the same state twice. For two alleles, $1-p^2-q^2=2pq$. It increases with both allelic number and frequency evenness; the biallelic maximum is 1/2, although multiallelic values can approach one. Do not sum $2p_j(1-p_j)$ over all states without dividing by two.

For a sample of $n$ chromosomes, frequencies $\hat p_j$ describe drawing with replacement. Comparing distinct sampled chromosomes instead gives the finite-sample correction


$$
h=\frac{n}{n-1}\left(1-\sum_j\hat p_j^2\right).
$$


At a biallelic site with derived count $i$, $h=2i(n-i)/[n(n-1)]$. This is an expected diversity statistic, not necessarily the observed fraction of heterozygous diploid individuals. The correction is verified in Hahn 3.1 and explains the slides' equality between site heterozygosity and pairwise diversity.

The finite-sample corrected h is an estimator rather than the population parameter: in a two-chromosome sample with different alleles it equals 1, although a biallelic population H cannot exceed 1/2. Sampling estimates need not remain within every bound of their target parameter.
Pairwise differences and segregating sites

For $n$ aligned sequences, $k_{uv}$ counts nucleotide differences between sequences $u$ and $v$. For $L$ callable aligned sites and $S$ polymorphic sites,


$$
\pi_{\rm locus}=\frac{\sum_{u<v}k_{uv}}{\binom n2}=\sum_{j=1}^{L}h_j,\qquad \pi_{\rm site}=\pi_{\rm locus}/L.
$$


There are $n(n-1)/2$ pairs. A site at intermediate frequency contributes more pairwise differences than a singleton. Another statistic counts polymorphic positions regardless of frequency:


$$
a_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac1i,\qquad \hat\theta_W=\frac{S}{a_n},\qquad \hat\theta_{W,\rm site}=\frac{S}{a_nL}.
$$


The harmonic correction follows the neutral expectation $E[S]=\theta a_n$, later derived from genealogy in Lecture 5. Here $\theta=4N_e\mu$ with mutation rate $\mu$ per locus per generation, or per site if all quantities are divided by $L$. The statistic is always calculable, but estimates that model parameter only under neutrality, constant-size panmixia and an infinite-sites mutation model. $E[\pi]=E[\hat\theta_W]=\theta$ does not mean their observed values must match.

If missing data change sample size at site $j$, use $n_j$ in its heterozygosity or harmonic correction and an explicit callable-site policy. Pairwise deletion and complete-site exclusion need not give the same result. A gap, missing genotype or unsequenced base is not an invariant observation.
Constructing the frequency spectrum

Define $\xi_i$ (the slides also use $S_i$) as the number of sites whose derived allele occurs $i$ times among $n$ sampled chromosomes, $i=1,\ldots,n-1$. Then


$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\xi_i,\qquad \pi=\frac{\sum_i i(n-i)\xi_i}{\binom n2}.
$$


An outgroup can suggest the ancestral state, but recurrent mutation, ancestral polymorphism or disagreement among outgroups can make polarization uncertain. The derived allele need not be the minor one. Without reliable polarity, fold counts: $\eta_i=\xi_i+\xi_{n-i}$ for $i<n/2$, and $\eta_{n/2}=\xi_{n/2}$ once when $n$ is even. Folding loses the distinction between a new rare mutation and a nearly fixed derived variant.

A joint spectrum $\xi_{ij}$ counts a site's derived copies in two populations of sizes $n_1,n_2$. Interior cells represent shared polymorphism; edges with a zero count in one population include private variants; boundary/corner cells can also represent fixed differences, depending on the included sites. More recent splits and more migration can both enrich sharing, so the slide's 2D galleries require a model rather than a single diagnostic shape. Lecture 7 develops that comparison.

The now-verified joint-SFS gallery uses additional scaled parameters: ancestral diploid size $N_A$, descendant sizes $N_1=\nu_1N_A,N_2=\nu_2N_A$, time $\tau=t/(2N_A)$, mutation input $\theta=4N_A\mu$ and symmetric migration parameter $M_{\rm mig}=2N_Am$. The figure calls this migration parameter M; it is **not** our earlier gene-copy count M and differs from the 4Nem convention in the island approximation. The gallery compares ν pairs (0.5,0.5) and (0.9,0.1), elapsed scaled times 0.1,0.3,1, and migration settings 0.1,2,10. Drift broadens frequencies; migration tends to pull each population toward the other, increasing sharing; mutation enters along axes, while loss/fixation moves sites toward boundary states.

For an original numerical translation, NA=10,000,ν1=0.9,ν2=0.1 gives sizes 9,000 and 1,000. At t=6,000 generations, τ=0.3. With m=0.0001 per generation, Mmig=2, not two gene copies and not necessarily two successful migrants. With μ=10⁻⁸ per site, theta=0.0004 per site. These scaling choices explain why plots with the same physical populations cannot be compared using different M definitions without conversion.
Singleton and high-frequency estimators: resolving the notation

Under the neutral infinite-sites model $E[\xi_i]=\theta/i$. Derived singletons alone therefore estimate $\theta$ by $\hat\theta_e=\xi_1$. **Correction to slide 17:** Hahn printed p.49 defines $\eta_1$ (for n>2 with the distinct singleton/complement classes used here) using folded singleton counts $S_1^*=\xi_1+\xi_{n-1}$, not just derived singletons:


$$
\hat\theta_\eta=\frac{n-1}{n}S_1^*.
$$


Its expectation is $[(n-1)/n][\theta+\theta/(n-1)]=\theta$. Applying that correction to derived singletons alone would bias the result downward.

Hahn and the slides define a statistic emphasizing high-frequency derived variants:


$$
\hat\theta_H=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}i^2\xi_i}{\binom n2}.
$$


Substitute $E[\xi_i]=\theta/i$: its expectation becomes $\theta\sum_i i/\binom n2=\theta$. Unlike $\pi$, its contribution is not symmetric under $i\leftrightarrow n-i$; polarization errors can severely inflate it. In T2 it enters Fay and Wu's $H=\pi-\hat\theta_H$.

To exclude **derived** singletons suspected of error, define $S_{\rm multi}=S-\xi_1$ and use


$$
\hat\theta_{W,\rm multi}=\frac{S-\xi_1}{a_n-1}.
$$


The denominator subtracts their expected $\theta$ contribution. This needs $n>2$ and correct polarity. If instead removing both folded singleton classes at $n>2$, the neutral denominator is $a_n-1-1/(n-1)$, when positive. Hahn's supplementary pairwise correction is $\hat\theta_{\pi,\rm multi}=\pi_{\rm multi}n/(n-2)$. Neither strategy removes correlated multichromosome errors, and both discard genuine biological rare variants. Do not describe filtering as proof that removed calls were erroneous.
Empirical diversity and model limits

The slides compare silent-site diversity across species: $\pi_{\rm site}=0.005$ means an average of five differences per 1,000 callable bases between distinct sampled sequences. It is not five variants in every individual. Maize diversity varies among genomic regions, so a genome mean can hide substantial heterogeneity. In the *Arabidopsis kamchatica* example, the illustrated synonymous spectrum has fewer low-frequency variants relative to the compared functional category in a polyploid context; copy counting and variant calling must respect ploidy, and functional categories need not share selection histories.

The infinite-sites model assumes each mutation hits a previously unmutated position; recurrent hits can hide substitutions and make $S$ underestimate mutation events. Sequencing errors can increase $S$ through spurious singletons. Selection, structure and changing size alter the spectrum even with flawless calls. Report both amount and frequency distribution, compare matched site categories, and explain callable-site and ancestral-state policies before inferring why diversity varies.

Functional constraint can keep nonsynonymous mutations rare, while synonymous sites provide a different reference spectrum; polyploid history and site ascertainment also affect the comparison. A category contrast motivates selection hypotheses but is not by itself a unique estimate of purifying fitness effects.

lessons.aiPrompt:
Explain and apply Quantifying molecular diversity using the following authored course reference.
Diversity as a probability
A gene-diversity measure asks whether two randomly drawn copies differ. With population allele frequencies $p_j$, $H=1-\sum_j p_j^2$: subtract the probability of drawing the same state twice. For two alleles, $1-p^2-q^2=2pq$. It increases with both allelic number and frequency evenness; the biallelic maximum is 1/2, although multiallelic values can approach one. Do not sum $2p_j(1-p_j)$ over all states without dividing by two.

For a sample of $n$ chromosomes, frequencies $\hat p_j$ describe drawing with replacement. Comparing distinct sampled chromosomes instead gives the finite-sample correction


$$
h=\frac{n}{n-1}\left(1-\sum_j\hat p_j^2\right).
$$


At a biallelic site with derived count $i$, $h=2i(n-i)/[n(n-1)]$. This is an expected diversity statistic, not necessarily the observed fraction of heterozygous diploid individuals. The correction is verified in Hahn 3.1 and explains the slides' equality between site heterozygosity and pairwise diversity.

The finite-sample corrected h is an estimator rather than the population parameter: in a two-chromosome sample with different alleles it equals 1, although a biallelic population H cannot exceed 1/2. Sampling estimates need not remain within every bound of their target parameter.

Pairwise differences and segregating sites
For $n$ aligned sequences, $k_{uv}$ counts nucleotide differences between sequences $u$ and $v$. For $L$ callable aligned sites and $S$ polymorphic sites,


$$
\pi_{\rm locus}=\frac{\sum_{u<v}k_{uv}}{\binom n2}=\sum_{j=1}^{L}h_j,\qquad \pi_{\rm site}=\pi_{\rm locus}/L.
$$


There are $n(n-1)/2$ pairs. A site at intermediate frequency contributes more pairwise differences than a singleton. Another statistic counts polymorphic positions regardless of frequency:


$$
a_n=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac1i,\qquad \hat\theta_W=\frac{S}{a_n},\qquad \hat\theta_{W,\rm site}=\frac{S}{a_nL}.
$$


The harmonic correction follows the neutral expectation $E[S]=\theta a_n$, later derived from genealogy in Lecture 5. Here $\theta=4N_e\mu$ with mutation rate $\mu$ per locus per generation, or per site if all quantities are divided by $L$. The statistic is always calculable, but estimates that model parameter only under neutrality, constant-size panmixia and an infinite-sites mutation model. $E[\pi]=E[\hat\theta_W]=\theta$ does not mean their observed values must match.

If missing data change sample size at site $j$, use $n_j$ in its heterozygosity or harmonic correction and an explicit callable-site policy. Pairwise deletion and complete-site exclusion need not give the same result. A gap, missing genotype or unsequenced base is not an invariant observation.

Constructing the frequency spectrum
Define $\xi_i$ (the slides also use $S_i$) as the number of sites whose derived allele occurs $i$ times among $n$ sampled chromosomes, $i=1,\ldots,n-1$. Then


$$
S=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\xi_i,\qquad \pi=\frac{\sum_i i(n-i)\xi_i}{\binom n2}.
$$


An outgroup can suggest the ancestral state, but recurrent mutation, ancestral polymorphism or disagreement among outgroups can make polarization uncertain. The derived allele need not be the minor one. Without reliable polarity, fold counts: $\eta_i=\xi_i+\xi_{n-i}$ for $i<n/2$, and $\eta_{n/2}=\xi_{n/2}$ once when $n$ is even. Folding loses the distinction between a new rare mutation and a nearly fixed derived variant.

A joint spectrum $\xi_{ij}$ counts a site's derived copies in two populations of sizes $n_1,n_2$. Interior cells represent shared polymorphism; edges with a zero count in one population include private variants; boundary/corner cells can also represent fixed differences, depending on the included sites. More recent splits and more migration can both enrich sharing, so the slide's 2D galleries require a model rather than a single diagnostic shape. Lecture 7 develops that comparison.

The now-verified joint-SFS gallery uses additional scaled parameters: ancestral diploid size $N_A$, descendant sizes $N_1=\nu_1N_A,N_2=\nu_2N_A$, time $\tau=t/(2N_A)$, mutation input $\theta=4N_A\mu$ and symmetric migration parameter $M_{\rm mig}=2N_Am$. The figure calls this migration parameter M; it is **not** our earlier gene-copy count M and differs from the 4Nem convention in the island approximation. The gallery compares ν pairs (0.5,0.5) and (0.9,0.1), elapsed scaled times 0.1,0.3,1, and migration settings 0.1,2,10. Drift broadens frequencies; migration tends to pull each population toward the other, increasing sharing; mutation enters along axes, while loss/fixation moves sites toward boundary states.

For an original numerical translation, NA=10,000,ν1=0.9,ν2=0.1 gives sizes 9,000 and 1,000. At t=6,000 generations, τ=0.3. With m=0.0001 per generation, Mmig=2, not two gene copies and not necessarily two successful migrants. With μ=10⁻⁸ per site, theta=0.0004 per site. These scaling choices explain why plots with the same physical populations cannot be compared using different M definitions without conversion.

Singleton and high-frequency estimators: resolving the notation
Under the neutral infinite-sites model $E[\xi_i]=\theta/i$. Derived singletons alone therefore estimate $\theta$ by $\hat\theta_e=\xi_1$. **Correction to slide 17:** Hahn printed p.49 defines $\eta_1$ (for n>2 with the distinct singleton/complement classes used here) using folded singleton counts $S_1^*=\xi_1+\xi_{n-1}$, not just derived singletons:


$$
\hat\theta_\eta=\frac{n-1}{n}S_1^*.
$$


Its expectation is $[(n-1)/n][\theta+\theta/(n-1)]=\theta$. Applying that correction to derived singletons alone would bias the result downward.

Hahn and the slides define a statistic emphasizing high-frequency derived variants:


$$
\hat\theta_H=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}i^2\xi_i}{\binom n2}.
$$


Substitute $E[\xi_i]=\theta/i$: its expectation becomes $\theta\sum_i i/\binom n2=\theta$. Unlike $\pi$, its contribution is not symmetric under $i\leftrightarrow n-i$; polarization errors can severely inflate it. In T2 it enters Fay and Wu's $H=\pi-\hat\theta_H$.

To exclude **derived** singletons suspected of error, define $S_{\rm multi}=S-\xi_1$ and use


$$
\hat\theta_{W,\rm multi}=\frac{S-\xi_1}{a_n-1}.
$$


The denominator subtracts their expected $\theta$ contribution. This needs $n>2$ and correct polarity. If instead removing both folded singleton classes at $n>2$, the neutral denominator is $a_n-1-1/(n-1)$, when positive. Hahn's supplementary pairwise correction is $\hat\theta_{\pi,\rm multi}=\pi_{\rm multi}n/(n-2)$. Neither strategy removes correlated multichromosome errors, and both discard genuine biological rare variants. Do not describe filtering as proof that removed calls were erroneous.

Empirical diversity and model limits
The slides compare silent-site diversity across species: $\pi_{\rm site}=0.005$ means an average of five differences per 1,000 callable bases between distinct sampled sequences. It is not five variants in every individual. Maize diversity varies among genomic regions, so a genome mean can hide substantial heterogeneity. In the *Arabidopsis kamchatica* example, the illustrated synonymous spectrum has fewer low-frequency variants relative to the compared functional category in a polyploid context; copy counting and variant calling must respect ploidy, and functional categories need not share selection histories.

The infinite-sites model assumes each mutation hits a previously unmutated position; recurrent hits can hide substitutions and make $S$ underestimate mutation events. Sequencing errors can increase $S$ through spurious singletons. Selection, structure and changing size alter the spectrum even with flawless calls. Report both amount and frequency distribution, compare matched site categories, and explain callable-site and ancestral-state policies before inferring why diversity varies.

Functional constraint can keep nonsynonymous mutations rare, while synonymous sites provide a different reference spectrum; polyploid history and site ascertainment also affect the comparison. A category contrast motivates selection hypotheses but is not by itself a unique estimate of purifying fitness effects.

lessons.title: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium as a null model
lessons.summary: Derive Hardy–Weinberg genotype proportions from random gamete union and use them as a precisely defined reference model.
objectives: Derive p², 2pq and q² and show allele conservation under segregation
Separate conditions for random-mating genotype proportions from conditions for unchanging allele frequencies
Diagnose possible deviations without equating a departure with selection
sections: Mendelian segregation does not by itself change allele frequency

A heterozygote contributes the two alleles equally in Mendelian meiosis. Random union of gametes produces diploid genotypes. Let $p$ be the probability of an $A$ gamete and $q=1-p$ that of $a$, with independent parental gamete states. Multiplying the two probabilities gives this mating table:

| | A with probability p | a with probability q |
|---|---|---|
| A with probability p | AA: p² | Aa: pq |
| a with probability q | Aa: qp | aa: q² |

The two heterozygote arrangements combine: $f_{AA}=p^2,f_{Aa}=2pq,f_{aa}=q^2$. The check is $(p+q)^2=1$. These are expectations under random gamete union, not exact finite-sample counts. In a geometric picture, a unit square has side segments $p$ and $q$; its four areas are exactly the four table entries.
Why allele frequencies are conserved

Count an $A$ copy once per AA genotype probability and half per heterozygote probability:


$$
p'=f_{AA}'+\frac12 f_{Aa}'=p^2+pq=p(p+q)=p.
$$


Similarly $q'=q^2+pq=q$. Iterating gives $p_t=p_0$ if no additional forces change gamete composition. One random-mating generation generates HWE proportions even from non-HWE starting genotypes, provided the relevant male/female gamete pools have the same frequencies. If the pools differ, heterozygote frequency is $p_{\rm male}q_{\rm female}+q_{\rm male}p_{\rm female}$ instead.

Heterozygosity $H(p)=2p(1-p)$ has derivative $2-4p$, zero at $p=1/2$, and second derivative $-4<0$. Its maximum is 1/2. A newly arisen diploid autosomal allele is usually in a heterozygote simply because its frequency is tiny; this is not a claim about dominance of its phenotype.
Assumptions: proportions versus no evolution

The slides list infinite size, random mating (panmixia), no mutation, no migration and equal allelic contribution to descendants (no selection). Together these give a deterministic, unchanging reference. Infinite size suppresses drift; no mutation/migration/selection keep the gamete allele frequencies unchanged. Mendelian segregation is also implicit.

Random union is the immediate reason for $p^2,2pq,q^2$. Selection or migration can change $p$ yet random mating may still regenerate those proportions afterward. A population can be in HWE at a locus while it evolves in allele frequency. Conversely, selfing or inbreeding can alter genotype frequencies without immediately changing allele frequencies. Do not confuse absence of genotype disequilibrium with absence of all evolutionary processes.
Diagnosing a deviation in empirical samples

Expected counts are $Np^2,2Npq,Nq^2$. Estimate $p$ from counts, then compare observations to that fitted expectation. A supplementary Pearson check uses $\chi^2=\sum_g(O_g-E_g)^2/E_g$ over genotypes $g$; with estimated p the conventional large-sample degrees of freedom is one. Small expected counts require an appropriate exact test instead. Multiple loci require multiple-testing control. A rejection alone does not identify the mechanism.

Heterozygote deficiency can reflect selfing, related mating, pooled demes (Wahlund effect, Lecture 4), allele dropout/null alleles or selection. Excess may reflect disassortative mating or heterozygote advantage. Recheck genotype quality and sample structure before invoking adaptive explanations. The slides' historical overview of Darwin, Mendelian genetics, Fisher/Wright, Kimura and Ohta shows why an explicit neutral or nearly neutral null is necessary; historical prominence is not evidence for a mechanism at a particular locus.

Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. practice.question: Derive the HWE proportions using areas rather than memorizing the formula.
practice.solution: Partition both sides of a unit square into p and q; two homozygote squares have areas p² and q²; the two heterozygote rectangles each have area pq.

practice.question: Can migration change p without preventing HWE in offspring?
practice.solution: Yes. Migration changes the gamete pool; subsequent random gamete union gives HWE at the new p.

practice.question: Design two checks before interpreting a heterozygote deficit as selection.
practice.solution: Inspect allele balance/genotype call quality and stratify by location or ancestry. Evaluate finite-sample uncertainty; both errors and structure can create a deficit.

lessons.title: Drift as random sampling of gene copies
lessons.summary: Explain drift as repeated finite sampling and quantify frequency changes across replicate populations.
objectives: Derive allele-count and allele-frequency moments from Bernoulli sampling
Predict how size and initial frequency affect stochastic trajectories
Distinguish evolution in a population from uncertainty in sampling that population
sections: A sample of a sample: the mechanism of drift

Even equally fit organisms do not contribute exactly equal numbers of descendants. Gamete transmission and reproduction sample a finite pool of gene copies. Sampling again in the next generation makes small chance deviations inherited rather than immediately corrected. This is genetic drift: a non-directional stochastic change in allele frequencies, affecting every finite population.

The plant sequence examples in the current slides connect geographic isolation and ecological adaptation to genomic patterns, but demographic and selective causes are not identifiable from an alignment alone. Replicate populations starting at the same frequency follow different paths. Smaller populations usually spread more rapidly across frequency states and reach loss or fixation sooner. A rare allele may rise; neutrality does not mean it always declines.
From one Bernoulli draw to a generation

Use $M$ for gene copies: $M=N$ in a haploid model, $M=2N$ for diploid autosomal sampling. A Bernoulli indicator $Y_k$ is 1 if sampled copy $k$ is $A$, otherwise 0. With independent sampling with replacement, $E[Y_k]=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y_k)=p(1-p)$. The next-generation count is $X'=\sum_{k=1}^M Y_k$:


$$
E[X'\mid p]=Mp,\quad \operatorname{Var}(X'\mid p)=Mp(1-p).
$$


Divide by $M$ to get $p'=X'/M$. Variances scale by the square of a multiplier:


$$
E[p'\mid p]=p,\quad E[\Delta p\mid p]=0,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\Delta p\mid p)=\frac{p(1-p)}M.
$$


The mean is a conditional expectation over reproductive realizations. Frequency variance is dimensionless squared; the count variance is in copies squared. For diploid effective-size approximations replace $M$ by $2N_e$. These results assume neutral, independent random reproduction, no mutation/migration and fixed number of copies.
Why replicate distributions broaden

At $p=0$ or 1 variance is zero: the states are absorbing without mutation or immigration. At $p=1/2$, $pq=1/4$ is maximal; intermediate-frequency alleles have the largest absolute sampling variance. Relative fluctuations can nevertheless be especially important for rare alleles.

Under a neutral fixed-$M$ WF chain starting at $p_0$, the law of total variance and $E[p_t]=p_0$ give


$$
\operatorname{Var}(p_t)=p_0(1-p_0)\left[1-\left(1-\frac1M\right)^t\right].
$$


One derivation is to relate variance to expected diversity: $E[p_t(1-p_t)]=p_0q_0-\operatorname{Var}(p_t)$, while each reproductive generation multiplies that expectation by $1-1/M$. The distribution becomes increasingly concentrated at the absorbing endpoints. No finite set of replicates is guaranteed to have exactly the predicted mean or fraction fixed.
A practical simulation and empirical design

For the slide's six-copy example, start $i=4$, $p=4/6$. At each generation draw $X'\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(6,p)$, update $p=X'/6$, and repeat. Run many replicates and compare their mean, variance and endpoint counts. Repeat for $p_0=1/M$, and for larger $M$ at the same starting frequency; separate the effect of size from the effect of initial copy number.

The historical student material points to PopG and LearnPopGen. You can reproduce its logic in any binomial simulator without treating a single plotted path as an expectation. In empirical time series, drift variance, sequencing uncertainty, related samples and selection can all affect observed changes. Sample consistently and model observation error separately from biological transmission variance.

lessons.title: Fixation, loss, and absorption
lessons.summary: Separate neutral fixation probability, time to absorption, conditional fixation time and sojourn time.
objectives: Derive neutral fixation probability from a martingale or boundary equation
Calculate diffusion waiting-time approximations with correct signs and conditioning
Explain mutation input and why most new neutral copies are lost
sections: Loss, fixation and mutation supply

The absorbing endpoints are loss of $A$ ($p=0$) and fixation ($p=1$), in a finite model without recurrent mutation or immigration. Neutral frequency is a bounded martingale: $E[p_{t+1}\mid p_t]=p_t$. At eventual absorption, its value is either zero or one. Thus $E[p_\infty]=P(\text{fix})=p_0$, and loss probability is $1-p_0$. This is eventual probability, not the chance of fixing in the very next generation.

A new diploid autosomal mutation enters at $p_0=1/(2N)$; in a haploid population it enters at $1/N$. If the per-copy mutation probability is $\mu$, the expected number of new copies per generation is $M\mu$, not an unrestricted probability. Independent per-copy events give $P(\text{at least one})=1-(1-\mu)^M\approx M\mu$ only when $M\mu$ is small. Mutation supply and fixation chance are different quantities; Lecture 3 combines them into the neutral substitution rate.
Diffusion as a controlled approximation

When $N_e$ is large, discrete frequency steps can be approximated by a continuous stochastic process. Neutral mean increment is zero and variance per generation is $V(x)=x(1-x)/(2N_e)$. The backward generator on a smooth function $f$ is


$$
\mathcal Lf=\frac{x(1-x)}{4N_e}f''(x).
$$


The factor one half multiplying variance is essential. Fixation probability solves $\mathcal Lu=0$, with $u(0)=0,u(1)=1$, so $u''=0$ and $u=x$. This gives the same fixation probability as the exact neutral chain. Waiting times derived with this generator are **diffusion approximations in generations**, not exact finite-chain results.
Correcting the time expressions in the selection deck recap

Let $T_A$ be time until either boundary. Its mean $a(x)$ obeys $\mathcal La=-1$, $a(0)=a(1)=0$:


$$
a''(x)=-\frac{4N_e}{x(1-x)}=-4N_e\left(\frac1x+\frac1{1-x}\right).
$$


Integrate twice and apply the two boundaries:


$$
E[T_A\mid x]\approx-4N_e\{x\ln x+(1-x)\ln(1-x)\}.
$$


The logarithms are negative; the leading minus makes elapsed time positive. We use the continuous limits $x\ln x\to0$ at a boundary.

Conditioning changes the question. Define $g(x)=E[T_A\,1_{\rm fixation}\mid x]$. Then $\mathcal Lg=-u(x)=-x$, with zero boundary values, yielding $g=-4N_e(1-x)\ln(1-x)$. Divide by $u(x)=x$:


$$
E[T\mid\text{fix},x]\approx-4N_e\frac{1-x}{x}\ln(1-x).
$$


By allele-label symmetry,


$$
E[T\mid\text{loss},x]\approx-4N_e\frac{x}{1-x}\ln x.
$$


Their probability-weighted average equals $a(x)$. For a newly arisen mutation and $N=N_e\gg1$, conditional fixation time approaches $4N_e$ generations; unconditional absorption time is approximately $2[1+\ln(2N_e)]$. **Scientific correction:** the recap's negative $2N\ln(1/2N)$ cannot be a valid elapsed time; its “fixation”/“sojourn” labels must not be interchanged with these definitions.
Sojourn time is time spent at frequencies, not a guaranteed trajectory

A supplementary neutral diffusion occupancy density describes the expected generations spent in a small frequency interval near $y$, before absorption, starting at $x$:


$$
G(x,y)=\begin{cases}4N_e(1-x)/(1-y),&0<y<x,\\4N_e x/y,&x\le y<1.\end{cases}
$$


Then expected occupation of $[b,c]$ is $\int_b^cG(x,y)\,dy$; $G$ has units generations per unit frequency and integrating over (0,1) gives the absorption mean above. At $N_e=100,x=0.2$, expected time in $[0.5,0.6]$ is $80\ln(0.6/0.5)=14.5857$ generations. This average includes paths that never enter that interval. A sojourn density, mean allele age conditional on observing a present frequency, and a forward conditional fixation time are distinct quantities with distinct sampling assumptions.

These corrective derivations assume a constant neutral unstructured WF-equivalent population. Size change, selection or recurrent mutation requires different boundary problems. The slide's mention of allele age is therefore an invitation to specify a retrospective sampling model, not to use a negative time formula. Refer to the original Kimura–Ohta papers for conditioning conventions.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. $T_A$: first absorption in generations; T given fix/loss conditions on the eventual endpoint
$\mu$: mutation probability per copy per generation; $G(x,y)$: expected occupation-time density
lessons.workedExample: With $N_e=100$ and $p_0=0.2$, eventual fixation probability is 0.2. Absorption mean is $-400[0.2\ln(0.2)+0.8\ln(0.8)]=200.161$ generations. Conditional fixation mean is $-400(0.8/0.2)\ln(0.8)=357.030$; conditional loss mean is $-400(0.2/0.8)\ln(0.2)=160.944$. The weighted mean $0.2(357.030)+0.8(160.944)=200.161$ agrees. At $N=10,000,\mu=10^{-8}$ per site, new-mutation supply is $2N\mu=0.0002$ per generation and single-copy neutral fixation chance is $1/20,000$. A tiny chance does not imply a short successful trajectory.

assessment.explanation: $p_0=8/40=0.2$; 1/40 applies only to one copy.

lessons.title: Loss of heterozygosity and effective population size
lessons.summary: Derive expected diversity loss, half-life and variable-size effective population size without confusing expectations with trajectories.
objectives: Derive heterozygosity recurrence from ancestry and sampling variance
Calculate exact and approximate half-lives and variable-size products
Explain harmonic Ne, its approximation limits and different effective-size definitions
sections: Identity by descent and expected diversity

Two copies may be identical in state because they carry the same allele; identical by descent (IBD) means they inherit a specified ancestral copy. Without mutation, sharing a parent necessarily gives the same state. In WF diploids the probability of selecting the same parental copy is $c=1/(2N_e)$. If parents differ, their probability of different alleles is $H_t$, so


$$
E[H_{t+1}\mid H_t]=\left(1-\frac1{2N_e}\right)H_t.
$$


Equivalently, with current frequency p, $E[2p'(1-p')]=2\{E[p']-(E[p'])^2-\operatorname{Var}(p')\}=2pq(1-1/(2N_e))$. This variance derivation explains why a constant expected p does not imply constant expected H. An IBD recurrence is $F_{t+1}=c+(1-c)F_t$ relative to the chosen base population. IBD and allele diversity are related but not automatically interchangeable when mutation or base-population polymorphism matters.
Iteration, exponential approximation and half-life

With constant size and no mutation/migration,


$$
E[H_t]=H_0\left(1-\frac1{2N_e}\right)^t\approx H_0e^{-t/(2N_e)}.
$$


The exact expectation under ideal WF follows by iterating the multiplier; $\ln(1-z)\approx-z$ gives the large-size exponential approximation. The time for half the expected initial diversity is


$$
t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln(1/2)}{\ln(1-1/(2N_e))}\approx2N_e\ln2.
$$


These are generations. A locus can temporarily gain heterozygosity as frequency approaches 1/2; the expectation declines. Exponential loss has a constant proportional rate and a declining absolute slope, correcting the historical slide's “slowly then fast” wording. Diversity at finite t is not forced to have its exact expected value.
Fluctuating size and harmonic effective size

With diploid sizes $N_0,\ldots,N_{t-1}$:


$$
E[H_t]=H_0\prod_{g=0}^{t-1}\left(1-\frac1{2N_g}\right).
$$


Matching this product to a constant-size multiplier gives $\ln(1-1/(2N_e))=t^{-1}\sum_g\ln(1-1/(2N_g))$. If **every** size is sufficiently large, approximate each logarithm by $-1/(2N_g)$ to obtain


$$
N_e\approx\frac{t}{\sum_g 1/N_g}.
$$


Small sizes dominate this harmonic mean, so short bottlenecks can reduce retained diversity far more than the arithmetic mean suggests. A moving-window value changes as a bottleneck enters or leaves the window; it is not a universal, memory-free census history.

The historical exercise uses $N=10,000$ except one or ten generations at $N=1$ in a 40,000-generation window. Harmonic approximations are 8,000.16 and 2,857.35, respectively, but N=1 invalidates the large-N logarithm expansion: the exact bottleneck factors are $(1/2)$ and $(1/2)^{10}$. Those extreme examples teach the approximation's failure as well as bottleneck sensitivity. If the window excludes the bottleneck, its harmonic size returns to 10,000; lost alleles do not magically return. More generally, finite sizes at each generation do not alone guarantee eventual loss under unbounded growth: the cumulative coalescence hazard must diverge.

The historical reference to about 4Ne generations is an ancestral-time scale: expected sample MRCA height approaches 4Ne in the standard coalescent. It is not a sharp time after which all loci forget a bottleneck or regain lost variation; mutation, genealogy variance and sampling determine recovery.
Effective size is a model equivalence

Census N counts individuals; Ne is defined by matching a genetic process to an ideal population. Variance, inbreeding, eigenvalue and coalescent effective sizes agree under suitable equilibrium assumptions but can differ in nonequilibrium histories (Hahn p.6). Unequal reproductive success, sex ratio, overlapping generations, structure and linked selection can change those equivalences. Ne is often lower than census size, not mathematically required to be lower in every model.

The mutation-diversity relation $\theta=4N_e\mu$ gives $N_e=\theta/(4\mu)$ only if theta genuinely describes the neutral equilibrium model and mutation units are matched. A realized estimator such as pi is noisy; no exact realized identity $\pi=\theta=i\xi_i$ holds at every locus. Ne inferred from diversity and from a short-term allele-frequency time series need not summarize the same history.

lessons.title: The Wright–Fisher transition model
lessons.summary: Build and use the finite Wright–Fisher transition matrix, connecting binomial sampling to full probability distributions.
objectives: State the neutral WF assumptions and distinguish copy-count conventions
Calculate one-step and multi-step finite-state probabilities
Interpret distribution vectors and a one-diploid founder example
sections: A model purpose and a notation contract

The Wright–Fisher model supplies a controlled null for random transmission. It is useful for synchronized annual populations: each generation is completely replaced. Neutral versions assume fixed $M$ independently sampled gene copies, random reproduction with replacement, no selection, migration or recurrent mutation at the tracked locus. All copies are exchangeable parents. For diploid autosomal inheritance $M=2N$; the six-unit plant slide uses $M=6$ and calls that number N. We explicitly translate its units instead of silently inserting a factor of two.

Fisher and Wright independently developed this model. It is an approximation to biology: families, selfing, seed banks, sexual systems and skewed reproductive success can violate independent gene-copy sampling. Model adequacy depends on the question, not on whether every detail resembles an organism.
Derive the full transition distribution

Given count $i$ today, each independent copy tomorrow is A with probability $p_i=i/M$. Any specified pattern of $j$ successes and $M-j$ failures has probability $p_i^j(1-p_i)^{M-j}$. There are $\binom Mj=M!/[j!(M-j)!]$ such patterns, giving


$$
P_{ij}=P(X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t=i)=\binom Mj\left(\frac iM\right)^j\left(1-\frac iM\right)^{M-j},\quad 0\le j\le M.
$$


The binomial theorem guarantees each row sums to one. The displayed reversed inequality in the slide is corrected here. At i=0 or M, define the row as probability one at that same boundary, avoiding ambiguity in 0^0 at the endpoints. The law gives the entire range of outcomes, unlike a mean that cannot describe endpoint probabilities.
A Markov chain and repeated generations

P is an $(M+1)\times(M+1)$ matrix indexed by counts 0 through M. The next state depends on current count, not the rest of the past: the Markov property. A row distribution vector $\boldsymbol v_t$ lists the probability of each state, so


$$
\boldsymbol v_{t+1}=\boldsymbol v_tP,\qquad\boldsymbol v_t=\boldsymbol v_0P^t.
$$


Multiplication sums over all possible intermediate states. A distribution vector is not a set of genotype proportions observed simultaneously in one population. The boundary rows are absorbing; interior rows distribute probability broadly, including direct jumps to either endpoint. Exact finite matrices are computationally useful for small M, while large matrices motivate diffusion approximations in Lecture 2.
One heterozygous founder: a fully solvable exercise

The historical exercise idealizes one diploid individual supplying an infinite random gamete pool and one diploid replacement each generation. It is a selfing/random-union model, not a realistic obligately outcrossing one-individual population. With $M=2$, count states 0,1,2 correspond to aa,Aa,AA. Neutral transition matrix is


$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\1/4&1/2&1/4\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$


Starting from $\boldsymbol v_0=(0,1,0)$, $\boldsymbol v_1=(1/4,1/2,1/4)$ and $\boldsymbol v_2=(3/8,1/4,3/8)$. At generation t the probability of remaining heterozygous is $2^{-t}$, with each absorbing genotype probability $(1-2^{-t})/2$. At t=20, $P(Aa)=9.53674\times10^{-7}$. This explicitly connects matrix iteration to diversity loss and neutral fixation probability, without claiming the single population simultaneously contains all those genotypes.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. Loss probability next generation is $(1/3)^6=1/729=0.00137174$; fixation probability next generation is $(2/3)^6=64/729=0.0877915$. Eventual neutral fixation probability is instead 4/6. Expected count is 4, count variance $6(2/3)(1/3)=4/3$, and frequency variance $(4/3)/36=1/27$. The expected count is not a guarantee of j=4.

lessons.title: The Moran birth–death model
lessons.summary: Derive birth–death transitions and compare exact event-scale moments with generation-scale approximations.
objectives: Enumerate all Moran birth/death events and derive the self-loop
Calculate count/frequency moments and diversity loss per event
Explain why biological turnover time and matched drift time differ
sections: One replacement event with overlapping ages

A Moran population consists of M haploid units. Each event chooses a parent uniformly and independently chooses a unit to die, with replacement, so the same unit may be chosen for both. Copy count changes by at most one; population size stays M. Individuals of different ages can coexist, making this an overlapping-turnover model. An embedded discrete event chain can be put on a continuous clock by assigning a Poisson event rate, but that clock is an additional convention.

To compare with diploid autosomal WF, we may use M=2N units; this does not turn the underlying haploid birth–death mechanism into a realistic diploid mating system. Hahn uses 2N haploid units for this comparison; current slides use N for unit count. We use M consistently.
Four disjoint possibilities and the tridiagonal matrix

With $p=i/M,q=1-p$, A parent/a death increases i with probability pq; a parent/A death decreases it with probability qp. A/A and a/a produce no change, with probabilities p² and q². Therefore


$$
P_{i,i+1}=P_{i,i-1}=pq,\qquad P_{ii}=p^2+q^2=1-2pq.
$$


All other one-event transitions are zero. The slide self-loop label j=1 is corrected to j=i. The three probabilities sum to one and become a pure self-loop at either endpoint. Choosing distinct parent/death units instead would change denominators and define a different model.
Exact event moments and expected heterozygosity

Let $\Delta i$ take values +1,−1,0. Then $E[\Delta i]=pq-pq=0$, $E[(\Delta i)^2]=2pq$, and


$$
E[i']=i,\quad \operatorname{Var}(i'\mid i)=2pq,\quad\operatorname{Var}(p'\mid p)=\frac{2pq}{M^2}.
$$


Substitute those moments in $E[2p'(1-p')]$ as in Lecture 2:


$$
E[H_{k+1}\mid H_k]=H_k\left(1-\frac{2}{M^2}\right),\qquad E[H_k]=H_0\left(1-\frac{2}{M^2}\right)^k.
$$


Here k counts elementary events. This exact Moran multiplier differs from the WF multiplier 1−1/M per whole generation. Diversity is lost on average although event frequency has no directional mean change.
Generation conventions and a finite-size correction to textbook shorthand

M events are often called one turnover generation: M births occur, but some units reproduce or die repeatedly while others survive. It is not guaranteed complete replacement. After k events the exact conditional-on-initial-p frequency variance is


$$
\operatorname{Var}(p_k\mid p_0)=p_0q_0\left[1-\left(1-\frac2{M^2}\right)^k\right].
$$


At k=M, this is approximately 2p0q0/M for large M, twice WF one-generation variance p0q0/M. Hahn p.5 states the generation-scale expression; we identify it as large-M shorthand for the event chain, not an exact finite-M multi-event variance. If matching drift rates instead of turnover, about M/2 Moran events match one WF generation to leading order. Exact diversity-rate matching uses $k=\ln(1-1/M)/\ln(1-2/M^2)$, which is generally not an integer.

Thus “Moran generations” must always include the event-rate convention. A continuously growing microbial population or overlapping-age organism may motivate turnover, but nonconstant size and correlated reproduction require extensions. A good simulation holds M fixed, repeatedly chooses the two independent types, and records unchanged events as well as upward/downward ones.

lessons.title: Wright–Fisher, Moran, and model choice
lessons.summary: Connect finite-model fixation, mutation supply and molecular substitution, and choose a model with explicit time scaling.
objectives: Derive the birth–death fixation product-sum solution and its neutral limit
Explain k=μ and distinguish molecular-clock evidence from universal neutrality
Connect forward transmission with backward shared ancestry and justify model choice
sections: Solve fixation from the birth–death recurrence

Let $u_i$ be eventual A-fixation probability from i copies in an M-unit birth–death chain; let $\alpha_i,\beta_i$ be one-step increase/decrease probabilities. The self-loop probability is $1-\alpha_i-\beta_i$. With $u_0=0,u_M=1$,


$$
u_i=\alpha_i u_{i+1}+(1-\alpha_i-\beta_i)u_i+\beta_i u_{i-1}.
$$


Rearrange to $\alpha_i(u_{i+1}-u_i)=\beta_i(u_i-u_{i-1})$. Set $d_i=u_i-u_{i-1}$ and $\gamma_i=\beta_i/\alpha_i$ for interior states. Then $d_{i+1}=\gamma_i d_i$, so $d_{j+1}=d_1\prod_{k=1}^j\gamma_k$. Sum increments to $u_M-u_0=1$:


$$
u_1=\left[1+\sum_{j=1}^{M-1}\prod_{k=1}^j\gamma_k\right]^{-1},
$$




$$
u_i=u_1\left[1+\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\prod_{k=1}^j\gamma_k\right].
$$


Neutral Moran has gamma=1, giving $u_1=1/M$ and $u_i=i/M$. This recurrence is exact for the specified finite birth–death chain. It is not a tridiagonal recurrence for full-generation WF, whose count jumps are larger. The selected constant-gamma extension appears in Lecture 6.
Mutation is not substitution: the neutral clock

Mutation introduces a new allele; substitution records an allele that has fixed. At diploid census size N and neutral mutation rate μ per site per generation, $E[\text{new copies}]=2N\mu$. Each neutral single copy has fixation probability $1/(2N)$, so long-run expected substitution rate is


$$
k=(2N\mu)\frac1{2N}=\mu.
$$


This equilibrium rate does not depend on N under the neutral model: larger populations supply more mutations but each has less chance to fix. It does not say mutations fix instantly; the successful trajectories can be long. Two independent lineages accumulating neutral substitutions for t generations have expected divergence $2\mu t$ under low divergence/infinite sites; ancestral polymorphism adds an additional term (T2).

If ν is the total mutation rate and only a fraction f0 is neutral, the neutral contribution is $k_0=f_0\nu$. The slide's molecular-clock plots motivate neutral molecular evolution but do not establish a universal constant amino-acid rate, nor that all molecular mutations are neutral. Constraint, generation times, mutation rates and adaptation can alter observed rates. Kimura's neutral and Ohta's nearly neutral interpretations concern distributions of fitness effects as well as drift.
Turn time around: the coalescent bridge

In diploid WF, given one sampled gene copy's parent, a second selects the same parent with probability $1/(2N_e)$. With constant size the exact pair waiting time is geometric with mean $2N_e$ generations. This backward ancestry calculation avoids simulating every nonsampled descendant. It motivates Lecture 5's sample genealogies; it is not the same quantity as a forward fixation time.

For Moran ancestry, shared-parent probabilities depend on the event clock. In one neutral M-unit event, two distinct sampled lineages coalesce with probability $2/M^2$: either lineage can be the replacement and trace to the other. Their mean pair waiting is $M^2/2$ events, or M/2 turnover generations when M events define one generation. Compare with WF M generations at the same copy count, which exposes the factor-of-two drift difference. Using $1/(2N)$ per unscaled Moran event would be a convention error.
Which model fits the biological question?

WF naturally represents synchronized nonoverlapping cohorts, such as annual seed-to-seed plants under a simplified no-seed-bank assumption. Moran represents continuous birth–death turnover at fixed size. Both have exchangeable neutral reproduction, absorbing endpoints and fixation probability equal to initial frequency. Their transitions, reproductive variance and clocks differ.

When interpreting data, state which outcome must be modeled: one-generation changes, lifetime fixation, genealogy or molecular substitutions. Then ask whether random reproduction, constant size and neutrality are adequate. Adding mutation, selection, structure or variable size changes the transition law or boundaries; it should answer a biological question rather than merely produce a more elaborate simulator.

lessons.title: Population subdivision and the Wahlund effect
lessons.summary: Explain pooled heterozygote deficits through allele-frequency variance and distinguish statistical mixture from biological fusion.
objectives: Calculate weighted pooled and within-deme diversity
Derive the Wahlund genotype-frequency and variance relationships
Interpret population fusion and recessive-homozygote examples without confusing structure with local inbreeding
sections: Local equilibrium is not pooled equilibrium

A deme is a locally interbreeding subpopulation. Restricted gene flow permits demes to diverge by drift and sometimes different selection. A region can contain multiple demes; an entire sampled area can contain multiple regions. HWE applies to the mating pool, not to any arbitrary collection of genotypes.

In the slide's extreme mouse example, one deme is fixed AA and another fixed aa. Each is locally in HWE (there is no polymorphism), yet an equal pooled sample has p=0.5 and no heterozygotes. Pooled HWE would predict 50% heterozygotes. This deficit caused by mixing allele frequencies is the Wahlund effect. It does not imply mating among relatives within the demes.
A weighted derivation

Let deme frequencies be $p_d$, weights $w_d\ge0$ summing to one, pooled frequency $\bar p=\sum_dw_dp_d$, $\bar q=1-\bar p$, and weighted frequency variance $V_p=\sum_dw_d(p_d-\bar p)^2$. Define


$$
H_S=\sum_dw_d2p_d(1-p_d),\qquad H_T=2\bar p\bar q.
$$


Since $\sum w_dp_d^2=\bar p^2+V_p$,


$$
H_S=2\bar p-2(\bar p^2+V_p)=H_T-2V_p.
$$


Under HWE within each deme, pooled genotype proportions become


$$
f_{AA}=\bar p^2+V_p,\quad f_{Aa}=2\bar p\bar q-2V_p,\quad f_{aa}=\bar q^2+V_p.
$$


Each homozygote increases by Vp relative to pooled HWE. This uses the weighted population variance, not automatically an n−1 unbiased sample-variance estimator. Weights specify the target: equal demes, equal regions or numbers of sampled individuals yield different questions. Sampling corrections for an estimated FST are a separate matter.
Pooling versus fusion: a recessive example

Statistical pooling does not change anyone's genotype. If separated demes actually interbreed at random, offspring instead have HWE at the pooled frequency. For a recessive allele a at frequencies q1,q2 in equally weighted demes,


$$
R_{\rm separate}-R_{\rm fused}=\frac{q_1^2+q_2^2}{2}-\bar q^2=V_q,
$$


where R is the aa proportion. Since Vp=Vq for two alleles, total homozygosity decreases by 2Vp and heterozygosity increases by that amount on random fusion. Environmental effects, penetrance and genotype-specific survival mean this genotype calculation is not automatically a clinical disease-risk prediction.

The slide lists cystic-fibrosis, sickle-cell and albinism allele-frequency illustrations (q≈0.022,0.05,0.07 in particular historical groups). They demonstrate how unequal recessive frequencies affect pooled expectations; they are not current medical prevalence estimates. With q1=0.1,q2=0.3, separate mean aa frequency is (0.01+0.09)/2=0.05; fused qbar²=0.04. The difference 0.01 is the frequency variance.
Structure in real sampling

Hierarchies can arise from geography and dispersal, as in the river-system illustration. A heterozygote deficit can also arise from selfing, inbreeding, genotyping error or selection; diagnosing the Wahlund effect requires evidence of differentiated mating pools. Inspect sample geography and ancestry, local HWE and genotype quality. The [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical) contains the existing workspace for the Linanthus/structure exercise; the private worksheet itself is not embedded in the app.

Link to [FST](/lesson/l4-fst) for normalization of this deficit and to [T1](/lesson/t1-ld-recombination) for mixture-generated associations between loci. Those associations may arise even on different chromosomes.

lessons.title: FST as a measure of differentiation
lessons.summary: Partition diversity across demes and regions, derive F-statistic relationships and interpret differentiation as a model-dependent statistic.
objectives: Compute FSR,FRT,FST with explicit hierarchical weights
Relate FST to allele-frequency variance and isolation time
Interpret finite-sample estimators, thresholds and crop examples cautiously
sections: What is standardized by FST?

Raw among-deme frequency variance is greatest when pooled allele frequency is intermediate. To compare relative differentiation, divide by the maximum variance at that pooled frequency:


$$
F_{ST}=\frac{H_T-H_S}{H_T}=\frac{V_p}{\bar p\bar q}.
$$


The equivalence follows HT−HS=2Vp and HT=2pbar qbar. Frequencies fixed identically in every deme give HT=0; FST is then undefined, not evidence of maximal differentiation. In this population-level diversity formulation FST ranges 0–1, reaching one for alternative fixed states across demes. Sampling-corrected estimators can be slightly negative; that indicates estimation variability rather than negative biological differentiation.

Different statistics called FST have different weighting and finite-sample corrections. A descriptive ratio of pooled heterozygosities is not automatically an unbiased Weir–Cockerham estimator. Marker diversity, ascertainment and small sample sizes affect comparisons. High FST does not mean a fixed proportion of individuals are migrants or a percentage of genes are different.
Deme, region and total: the slides’ notation

Let region r have weight Wr, and its demes have conditional weights w(d|r). Calculate regional mean pbar_r, regional random-mating diversity $2\bar p_r(1-\bar p_r)$, and


$$
H_R=\sum_rW_r2\bar p_r(1-\bar p_r),\quad H_S=\sum_rW_r\sum_dw(d\mid r)2p_d(1-p_d).
$$


HT uses the weighted grand mean. The taught regional statistics are


$$
F_{SR}=\frac{H_R-H_S}{H_R},\quad F_{RT}=\frac{H_T-H_R}{H_T},\quad F_{ST}=\frac{H_T-H_S}{H_T}.
$$


S denotes subpopulations, R regions and T total. Taking complements gives $1-F_{ST}=(1-F_{SR})(1-F_{RT})$, hence $F_{ST}=F_{SR}+F_{RT}-F_{SR}F_{RT}$. They do not simply add. Individual-level FIS/FIT are supplementary related quantities, not replacements for the slide's regional definitions.
Working through the supplied practical

The Linanthus flower-colour dataset has six western, twenty central and four eastern demes. Under **equal-deme** weights, region weights are 6/30,20/30,4/30 rather than equal thirds. Compute each local 2p(1−p), average within regions, then calculate regional diversity from each regional mean. Taking a diversity of a mean and a mean of diversities are different operations; their difference carries the structure signal.

The source's rounded benchmark is HS=0.1424,HR=0.1589,HT=0.2371, giving FSR≈0.1038,FRT≈0.3298,FST≈0.3994 when unrounded data are used. Retain underlying precision before rounding; this is a worked numerical benchmark, not publication of the private solution document.

The second worksheet labels genotype entries “frequencies” although they are counts: two 60-individual samples with counts (20,20,20) and (15,15,30) imply p1=0.5,p2=0.375. Local expected diversity, not observed heterozygote fractions, enters this descriptive FST calculation. A third sample (20,25,15) has p3=65/120. The worked example below independently calculates the unrounded results.
Differentiation through time and empirical interpretation

In a simplified drift-only isolation model with initially undifferentiated constant-size diploid demes, the slide presents


$$
E[F_{ST}(t)]\approx1-e^{-t/(2N_e)}.
$$


It expresses accumulating relative differentiation as local diversity decays; exponential form is a large-size approximation. It is not a generally exact expectation of a ratio for arbitrary finite samples or histories. With Ne=1000 and t=1000 generations, it gives 1−e^−0.5=0.393469. Migration, selection, unequal sizes and ancestral structure alter this prediction.

The slides include crop-versus-wild maize FST≈0.11, common-bean population comparisons and a human continental example≈0.069. These are historical illustrative comparisons, not universal reference levels. Their qualitative threshold slide prints 0.005 as the little/moderate boundary; we report that source discrepancy rather than impose a cutoff. Interpret differentiation continuously and compare matched markers, sampling schemes and justified null distributions. Drift, restricted migration and local selection can all generate high values; causal assignment requires additional evidence.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
variables: $H_S,H_R,H_T$: weighted diversity at subpopulation, regional and total levels
$W_r,w(d\mid r)$: region and conditional deme weights
$t$: isolation generations; $N_e$: diploid deme effective size; F values are dimensionless
lessons.workedExample: For the worksheet's two equal samples, pbar=(0.5+0.375)/2=0.4375. HS=[0.5+0.46875]/2=0.484375, HT=2(0.4375)(0.5625)=0.4921875. Thus FST=(0.4921875−0.484375)/0.4921875=0.0158730. Adding p3=65/120 gives pbar=17/36=0.472222, HS=0.48842593, HT=0.49845679 and FST=0.02012384. A larger number of sampled demes can change the descriptive differentiation target as well as precision; it is not necessarily evolution between measurements.

practice.question: Show why the hierarchical F values do not add.
practice.solution: Multiply (HS/HR)(HR/HT)=HS/HT, then express each as one minus its corresponding F.

practice.question: Explain why observed heterozygote counts were not used directly in the worksheet FST.
practice.solution: The defined HS is mean local HWE diversity from allele frequencies; actual heterozygote departures measure additional phenomena.

practice.question: What further evidence would you seek for a high-FST candidate?

lessons.summary: Model gene flow and interpret PCA and ancestry clustering as statistical descriptions with explicit assumptions.
objectives: Calculate migration mixing and cautiously use the island approximation
Explain genotype centering, covariance, eigenvectors and PC scores
Interpret STRUCTURE/ADMIXTURE, MCMC and K without equating clusters with literal ancestors
sections: Migration opposes divergence

If fraction m of a recipient mating pool comes from migrants at frequency pM, then $p'=(1-m)p+mp_M$ and $\Delta p=m(p_M-p)$. This accounting assumes the migrant fraction and source frequency apply to the contributing gene pool, not simply travelers counted in the field. The two arrows in the slides allow different directions/rates; actual migration changes both populations if their pools are coupled.

In a neutral infinite-island approximation with many equal-sized diploid demes, symmetric migration, constant sizes, low mutation and drift–migration equilibrium,


$$
F_{ST}\approx\frac1{1+4N_em}.
$$


The factor 4 reflects diploid coalescent/migration scaling. A useful heuristic is that coalescence rate 1/(2Ne) competes with either of two lineages migrating at total rate≈2m. It is not a general exact conversion from a realized empirical FST to migrants. Nem=0.25,0.5,1,2 predicts 0.5,0.3333,0.2,0.1111. Split time, source variation, asymmetry, selection and nonequilibrium histories can make the same observed ratio correspond to very different movement.
PCA: a quantitative dimensionality reduction

Genomic data have individuals as rows and markers as columns. Let X be a numeric genotype matrix and Z its column-centered version (often also variance-scaled; specify that choice). With n individuals, marker covariance is $C=Z^TZ/(n-1)$. An eigenvector v satisfies $Cv=\lambda v$; scores along that axis are $Zv$. Eigenvalue λ measures variance on the axis, so explained fraction is $\lambda/\sum_j\lambda_j$.

The slide's four-sample/three-marker illustration constructs a centered matrix, covariance, eigenvectors, scores and projections. To show that pipeline without copying its figure, consider a supplementary two-marker centered matrix with rows (−1,−1),(−1,1),(1,−1),(1,1). Columns sum to zero and $C=\operatorname{diag}(4/3,4/3)$; both axes explain 1/2 of total variance. Equal eigenvalues mean no unique preferred first direction. If instead all rows lie along (1,1), that diagonal axis captures all variance. In real genotype PCA, normalization and LD pruning change which regions dominate.

Full-resolution inspection confirms the slide covariance normalization and reconstruction pipeline. If eigenvectors form orthonormal columns V, $CV=V\Lambda$, scores are $T=ZV$, and the full reconstruction is $X=TV^T+\boldsymbol1\bar{\boldsymbol x}^{\,T}$. With only leading components, the reconstruction is an approximation; discard axes only after stating the variance lost.

For the slide's four color-indicator rows (1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1),(0,0,0), column means are each 1/4. Direct centered cross-products give diagonal covariance 1/4 and off-diagonal −1/12, namely $C=(1/3)I-(1/12)J$ with J the all-ones 3×3 matrix. The all-ones axis has eigenvalue 1/12; any two orthonormal axes with coordinate sum zero have eigenvalue 1/3. Total variance is 3/4, so explained fractions are 4/9,4/9,1/9 (rounded 44%,44%,11% in the figure). One valid leading vector (1,−1,0)/sqrt(2) projects the first centered row to 1/sqrt(2)=0.707107. Tied leading eigenvalues allow different but equivalent rotated PC coordinates; source rounding and its chosen orientation do not change these relationships.
What PC plots show and what they do not

PCA summarizes covariance, not a specified population-split model. The slides' global sample scatter and European geography examples show geographic alignment of PC scores, but sampling density, family relatedness, batch artifacts and LD can also create structure. Flipping an eigenvector changes signs but not biology. A PC is not an ancestry percentage; distances in a projection omit variation on excluded axes.

Inspect missingness, sample geography, relatedness and correlated marker blocks, and test robustness to pruning/scaling. For presentations, label explained variance and specify the matrix preprocessing. Clusters suggest hypotheses about demes, migration or ecological history; they do not decide which cause generated the pattern.
Model-based clustering and K

STRUCTURE jointly infers cluster allele frequencies and membership/admixture proportions, often using Bayesian MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo). Its standard model seeks HWE within clusters and approximate independence across loci; mixture can generate both HWE deficits and LD. ADMIXTURE uses related ancestry models with a different optimization approach; do not call both algorithms identical.

With K components, an individual's proportions sum to one, but the colors represent fitted statistical components conditional on K and sample choice. Eurasian and European bar plots in the slides change as K changes. Choose a parsimonious value capturing the major structure and report uncertainty, convergence/replicates and sensitivity. There need not be a single true K recoverable from every sampling scheme. Historical migration can be inferred only with additional models/evidence; a colored bar alone is not a dated migration event or a pure ancestral population.

Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. variables: $m$: gene-pool migrant fraction per generation; $p_M$: source A frequency; $N_e$: diploid deme size
$Z$: centered/scaled n-individual genotype matrix; C: covariance matrix
$v,\lambda$: eigenvector/eigenvalue; $K$: fitted ancestry-component number
lessons.workedExample: At local p=0.8, source pM=0.2 and m=0.1, $p'=0.9(0.8)+0.1(0.2)=0.74$: gene flow moves toward the source. If Ne=500,m=0.002 in the island model, Nem=1 and FST≈1/(1+4)=0.2. Algebraically inverting an empirical FST=0.2 gives Nem≈1 **only if** the model holds. For a PCA covariance $C=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvectors $(1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$ have eigenvalues 3 and 1; PC1 explains 3/4=75%. A centered row (1,1) has PC1 score $\sqrt2$ and PC2 score zero, a projection rather than a migrant fraction.
