lessons.moduleDescription: Genealogies, waiting times, diversity expectations, and the connection between samples and population history.
lessons.title: Coalescence of two lineages
lessons.summary: Trace sampled chromosomes backward, derive pairwise waiting times and connect genealogy to sequence differences.
objectives: Explain state/descent decoupling and exchangeability under neutrality
Derive exact geometric and limiting exponential pair coalescence
Translate ancestral branch exposure into expected mutations and diversity
sections: The population contains more history than a sample needs

Forward WF reproduction generates all descendants; a present sample depends only on the ancestors of its sampled copies. Prune nonsampled branches and trace the surviving lineages backward until they meet. A coalescent event occurs when two copies have the same ancestral gene copy. It is not necessarily the first common ancestor of the two organisms across their entire genomes.

The slides connect evolutionary processes to distributions of summary statistics, then observed patterns back to parameter estimates. Coalescent simulation is efficient because it generates sample genealogies without every unobserved individual's reproduction. Under neutrality, parents are exchangeable: their genotype labels, location or age do not affect reproduction in the standard unstructured model. State and descent can be separated: first generate a genealogy, then place mutations. Selection/structure can couple them and require extensions.
The exact two-lineage waiting distribution

Use a diploid autosomal WF population of effective size Ne with 2Ne possible parental copies, constant through time. Conditional on the first lineage's parent, the second chooses that same copy with probability $c=1/(2N_e)$. Surviving uncoalesced generations contribute factors 1−c:


$$
P(T_2=t)=(1-c)^{t-1}c,\quad t=1,2,\ldots,
$$




$$
P(T_2>t)=(1-c)^t,\quad E[T_2]=1/c=2N_e,\quad\operatorname{Var}(T_2)=(1-c)/c^2.
$$


The geometric distribution is memoryless under a constant c. T2 counts generations back to a shared copy. Diploid individual count and sample chromosome count are distinct: sampling n chromosomes does not change the population size Ne.
From generations to coalescent units

Let scaled waiting time be $\tau=T_2/(2N_e)$. As size grows, $(1-1/(2N_e))^{2N_e t}$ tends to $e^{-t}$. Therefore $\tau\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)$ in the standard coalescent limit, with mean and variance one. The exponential is a continuous approximation/limit; it does not replace the exact finite-generation geometric distribution by an exact continuous law.

The standard model assumes neutrality, constant effective size, random reproduction, no subdivision, and a single nonrecombining locus. Exchangeability underlies Kingman's construction. Different loci may have different genealogies through recombination; a gene tree is not automatically a species tree or a complete pedigree. A realized sample can coalesce sooner or later than its mean.
Genealogy plus mutation gives observed diversity

Two lineages contribute twice the pair waiting time to total branch exposure. With μ mutations per site per generation and a neutral infinite-sites model,


$$
E[k_{12}]=\mu E[2T_2]=4N_e\mu=\theta_{\rm site}.
$$


For a locus of L sites and uniform rate, $\theta_{\rm locus}=4N_e\mu L$. The same letter theta in the slides must be read with its mutation-rate units. Coalescence itself does not create a SNP; mutation changes states along branches, and mutations older than the sample MRCA are fixed within that sample rather than segregating.

This links Lecture 1's pi to genealogical depth. Low pi may indicate short trees, low mutation rate, selection or technical loss of calls; observing two identical sequences does not prove immediate coalescence. A useful exercise is to draw two ancestral branches, mark elapsed generations and add expected mutation counts separately from realized counts.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
variables: $T_2$: generations backward to common gene-copy ancestry; $\tau=T_2/(2N_e)$: scaled time
$N_e$: diploid model effective size; $\mu$: per-site per-generation mutation probability
$k_{12}$: differences between two sequences; $L$: locus length in callable bases
lessons.workedExample: At Ne=10,000, c=1/20,000=0.00005. Exact pair mean is 20,000 generations and variance $20,000^2-20,000=399,980,000$ generations squared. In the exponential approximation, probability of surviving 10,000 generations without coalescing is $e^{-0.5}=0.606531$ (exact $(0.99995)^{10,000}$ is close). With μ=$10^{-8}$ per site and L=1,000, expected pairwise differences are $2(20,000)(10^{-8})(1000)=0.4$. This average can coexist with many identical pairs and occasional more divergent pairs.

assessment.explanation: Two copies match one of 2Ne parents.

assessment.question: What is expected T2 at that size?
assessment.explanation: Geometric mean 1/c=2Ne.

assessment.question: At μ=10⁻⁸,Ne=10,000,L=1,000, what is expected pairwise difference count?
assessment.explanation: $4N_e\mu L=0.4$; 0.0004 is per-site diversity.

assessment.question: Which law is exact for finite-generation pair waiting under the stated WF model?
assessment.explanation: Independent generations with constant success c give (1−c)^(t−1)c.

assessment.question: Why can genealogy be simulated before mutational states in the standard model?
assessment.explanation: Neutral descent does not depend on allelic labels.
options: Neutral reproduction is exchangeable with respect to state

assessment.question: Two sampled sequences are identical. What follows about their genealogy?
assessment.explanation: Identity in state alone cannot fix a coalescence time.

assessment.question: Mutations older than the sample MRCA generally do not segregate among that sample under infinite sites.

practice.question: What is c for haploid effective size Nh?
practice.solution: 1/Nh; pair mean Nh generations. The diploid 2Ne denominator is a copy count.

practice.question: Why does mutation exposure contain two branches?
practice.solution: Both sampled lineages can acquire mutations before meeting; expected exposure is 2E[T2].

practice.question: Why does recombination obstruct a single tree for a whole chromosome?
practice.solution: Different positions can inherit through different ancestral paths, producing local genealogies.

lessons.title: Waiting times with k lineages
lessons.summary: Construct Kingman genealogies, derive waiting times and tree height, and quantify topology and ancestral-time variability.
objectives: Derive the k-pair merger rate and its limiting assumptions
Calculate MRCA mean/variance and distinguish height from total length
Explain random pair-merger topologies and exchangeability
sections: Many pairs increase the merger opportunity

With k extant lineages there are $\binom k2=k(k-1)/2$ potential merging pairs. The rare-event approximation to one-generation merger probability is $c_k\approx\binom k2/(2N_e)$. For specified three copies, a triple merger probability is $1/(2N_e)^2$; two distinct simultaneous pair mergers also have order $N_e^{-2}$. Under fixed sample size with Ne tending large, those vanish relative to binary mergers.

For finite WF, probability of no merger among k copies is exactly $\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-j/(2N_e))$ (when k≤2Ne). Its complement is not exactly the pair-rate approximation for arbitrary k. Rare collisions need roughly k² small relative to 2Ne; simply assuming “k is smaller than Ne” is not quantitative proof. There are three unlabelled rooted binary shapes with five leaves: root splits 1+4, with the four-leaf part either balanced (2+2) or ladder-like (1+3); or root splits 2+3. lessons.title: Coalescent expectations for molecular diversity
lessons.summary: Derive molecular diversity from total branch length, Poisson mutations and descendant-count weighting.
objectives: Derive expected tree length, S and the harmonic sample correction
Explain conditional Poisson mutation placement and two sources of variance
Derive E[xi_i]=theta/i and E[pi]=theta; apply folded and joint spectra
sections: Mutation dropping is conditional on a genealogy

Under infinite sites, each mutation affects a new site; place mutations along ancestral branches at rate μ per locus per generation. For a branch with length ℓ generations, its count K is Poisson with mean $\mu\ell$:


$$
P(K=k\mid\ell)=e^{-\mu\ell}(\mu\ell)^k/k!,\quad E[K\mid\ell]=\operatorname{Var}(K\mid\ell)=\mu\ell.
$$


In scaled length $\ell_*=\ell/(2N_e)$, that mean is $\theta\ell_*/2$ with $\theta=4N_e\mu$. A branch inherited by i sampled descendants generates a derived-count-i SNP. An external branch generates a singleton; an internal branch generates shared variation.

Coalescent waiting times and topology can be drawn independently in the standard model. Mutations on disjoint branches are independent **conditional on their lengths**, not unconditionally independent of the genealogy producing their means. Evolutionary variation among genealogies and mutational variation on a given genealogy both contribute to data uncertainty.
Total tree length and segregating sites

With k lineages alive for Tk, total branch exposure from that interval is kTk. Thus


$$
B=\sum_{k=2}^n kT_k,\quad E[B]=\sum_{k=2}^n k\frac{4N_e}{k(k-1)}=4N_e a_n,
$$




$$
a_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\frac1j\approx\ln n+\gamma,\qquad\gamma\approx0.57721.
$$


Unlike height, total length grows logarithmically with sampling. Since $S\mid B\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu B)$, $E[S]=\mu E[B]=\theta a_n$, deriving Watterson's $\hat\theta_W=S/a_n$. More sampled sequences discover more segregating sites even though underlying population theta is unchanged.

Supplementary variance illustrates the two sources: $\operatorname{Var}(S)=E[\mu B]+\operatorname{Var}(\mu B)=\theta a_n+\theta^2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}1/j^2$ under the no-recombination model. Independent exponential interval variances give the second term. Recombination changes genealogical covariance and this variance; it does not simply change the mutation rate.
The neutral frequency spectrum and pairwise expectation

Exchangeable binary genealogies yield expected total length subtending exactly i descendants, $E[B_i]=4N_e/i$. For intuition, every mutation is assigned to descendants of its branch; averaging uniform merger histories over waiting times gives the 1/i weighting. This result assumes neutral constant-size panmixia and infinite sites, not arbitrary trees:


$$
E[\xi_i]=\mu E[B_i]=\theta/i,\quad i=1,\ldots,n-1.
$$


The identity can also be checked by summing branch classes: $\sum_iE[B_i]=4N_ea_n$. Its singleton prediction is E[xi1]=theta. The observed spectrum is noisy and a declining expected shape is not an exact spectrum for every sample.

Substitute the expected spectrum into the Lecture 1 pairwise formula:


$$
E[\pi]=\frac1{\binom n2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}i(n-i)\frac\theta i=\frac\theta{\binom n2}\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(n-i)=\theta.
$$


Pairwise sampling consistency gives the same result by considering a random two-leaf subsample and its two branches. Watterson and pi agree in expectation but weight realized mutations differently.
Optional derivation of the 1/i spectrum

For a standard Kingman sample of n chromosomes, let $A_{k,i}$ be the number of the k remaining ancestors that subtend exactly i sampled descendants. The ordered positive descendant-size compositions at the k-lineage stage are uniform under the random-merger model. There are $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ such compositions; fixing the size of one branch to i leaves $\binom{n-i-1}{k-2}$ ways to assign the other positive sizes. Hence


$$
E[A_{k,i}]=k\frac{\binom{n-i-1}{k-2}}{\binom{n-1}{k-1}},\quad 2\le k\le n-i+1.
$$


Waiting intervals are independent of these pair-merger/topology choices. Multiply their mean $4N_e/[k(k-1)]$ by the expected number of class-i branches and sum:


$$
E[B_i]=4N_e\sum_{k=2}^{n-i+1}\frac{\binom{n-i-1}{k-2}}{(k-1)\binom{n-1}{k-1}}.
$$


To evaluate the sum, write $1/[(k-1)\binom{n-1}{k-1}]=\int_0^1x^{k-2}(1-x)^{n-k}\,dx$. This beta integral equals $(k-2)!(n-k)!/(n-1)!$, matching the factorial ratio. Set j=k−2 inside the sum: the binomial theorem reduces the summed integrand to $(1-x)^{i-1}[x+(1-x)]^{n-i-1}=(1-x)^{i-1}$. Its integral is 1/i, so $E[B_i]=4N_e/i$ and $E[\xi_i]=\mu E[B_i]=\theta/i$.

This composition calculation concerns descendant sizes at a lineage-count stage, not equally probable unlabelled final tree shapes. For n=4,i=2, the k=2 term is 1/3 and the k=3 term is 1/6; their sum is 1/2, so expected class-2 length is 2Ne. This explicit calculation checks the general 1/i result rather than relying on a diagram.
From alignments to spectra and empirical departures

The slides' six-genome alignment example collapses nucleotide identities into binary variation, counts derived occurrences and then plots the spectrum. For a single-population SFS, exact genomic position and between-site associations are discarded. With unknown polarity fold i with n−i, counting the n/2 class once. Joint spectra retain cross-population counts and distinguish private from shared variation, motivating Lecture 7.

A Fogo spectrum with many low-frequency variants prompts a demographic/selection question, not a unique answer. Growth, sweeps and purifying selection can enrich rare alleles; long-lived balanced lineages or mixture can enrich intermediate counts. Outgroup errors, missingness and SNP discovery schemes can distort those shapes. Expected spectrum diagrams describe hypotheses, not measured histories. The distinction between a specific completed sweep and the broader category of positive selection matters: adaptation from multiple origins or polygenic change may not give the classic single-origin pattern.

practice.question: Explain how one internal mutation can generate many variant copies but one segregating site.

lessons.title: Allele-frequency change under viability selection
lessons.summary: Normalize genotype fitness contributions, infer relative viability under explicit sampling assumptions and explain dominance and balancing mechanisms.
objectives: Derive allele-frequency change from genotype fitness weighting
Distinguish fitness coefficients, dominance and marginal new-mutation advantage
Interpret genotype-survival comparisons and a stable overdominant equilibrium
sections: Fitness is reproductive contribution relative to a reference

Mutation is the ultimate source of new states. A mutation's effect may be deleterious, neutral, beneficial or frequency-dependent in a particular environment/genetic background. Drift still acts on all these classes. Purifying selection removes harmful changes; positive selection increases favorable changes; balancing selection can maintain multiple alleles through overdominance, rare-allele advantage or environmental variation.

Relative genotype fitness w expresses expected survival/reproductive contribution, scaled to a stated reference. A coefficient is not an absolute survival probability unless that is explicitly measured. Scaling all fitnesses by the same positive factor leaves allele change unchanged. Phenotypic dominance need not equal dominance for fitness. Under a deleterious-a convention use wAA=1,wAa=1−hs_d,waa=1−s_d with sd>0; h=0,1/2,1 specifies recessive, additive and dominant deleterious effects.
The normalized viability recursion

Assume an autosomal diploid random-mating population with genotype proportions p²,2pq,q² before selection. Multiplying by fitness gives **unnormalized contributions**, not frequencies summing to one:


$$
\bar w=p^2w_{AA}+2pqw_{Aa}+q^2w_{aa}.
$$


Divide each contribution by mean fitness. A counts as two in AA and one in Aa, so


$$
p'=\frac{p^2w_{AA}+pqw_{Aa}}{\bar w},\qquad q'=1-p'.
$$


Subtract p and simplify to obtain


$$
\Delta p=\frac{pq[p(w_{AA}-w_{Aa})+q(w_{Aa}-w_{aa})]}{\bar w}.
$$


This deterministic recursion assumes frequencies and fitness contributions can be treated as expectations, no mutation/migration during the selection step, and an appropriate preselection mating model. In small populations realized survival/reproduction adds stochastic variance. If initial genotype proportions are not HWE, weight the observed proportions directly instead of inserting p²,2pq,q².
Viability inference and the wingfruit slide discrepancy

If E_g describes preselection expected genotype counts and O_g postselection survivors, relative viability is proportional to O_g/E_g. Normalize to a chosen genotype: $w_g=(O_g/E_g)/(O_{Aa}/E_{Aa})$. This works only with comparable stages, ascertainment and no unmodeled demographic mixing.

The wingfruit table gives observed counts 297,498,55 (sum 850), expected counts 661,466,98 (sum 1225), and a displayed total 1225. We explicitly retain the discrepancy: the total may refer to the preselection cohort, but the slide does not establish those stages. Consequently we do not present fitted s,t as established biological estimates. The proportional-survival method is explained with an internally consistent original example below. Source species naming also remains an instructor-review item. This does not block learning the well-defined model.
Heterozygote advantage and stable allele frequencies

For overdominance, let wAA=1−t,wAa=1,waa=1−s with s,t>0. Substituting in Δp gives a numerator $pq(qs-pt)$. The interior equilibrium solves qs=pt, or


$$
p^*=\frac{s}{s+t},\qquad q^*=\frac{t}{s+t}.
$$


Below p*, qs exceeds pt and A increases; above it A decreases. Both alleles can therefore persist deterministically. Finite drift can still cause loss, and changing fitnesses move the equilibrium. Negative frequency-dependent selection likewise can protect rare alleles, as at plant self-incompatibility loci and in host–parasite coevolution; these are mechanisms, not an instruction to call every intermediate-frequency allele balanced.

The neutral reference E[pi]=4Neμ describes genealogical mutation exposure from Lecture 5; selection changes those assumptions. Rejection of neutral diversity is not a direct measurement of viability fitness and does not uniquely show adaptation.

With p=0.4,q=0.6 and fitnesses 1,0.9,0.8, mean fitness is $0.16+2(0.24)(0.9)+0.36(0.8)=0.88$. Normalized genotype proportions are 0.181818,0.490909,0.327273; p′=$(0.16+0.216)/0.88=0.427273$, giving Δp=0.027273. Equal-proportion assumptions apply before selection, not necessarily after it.

lessons.title: Fixation probability under selection and drift
lessons.summary: Compare exact finite birth–death fixation with weak-selection WF diffusion and define the effect convention behind 2s.
objectives: Derive selected Moran transitions and constant-r fixation
Calculate fixation probabilities and the neutral limit without mixing N conventions
Explain early loss, effective neutrality and model-dependent modifiers
sections: An exact selected birth–death model

Suppose M haploid units compete to reproduce: A has relative fecundity r>0, a has fecundity 1, and death is uniformly random. Then


$$
\alpha_i=\frac{ri}{ri+M-i}\frac{M-i}{M},\quad\beta_i=\frac{M-i}{ri+M-i}\frac iM.
$$


Their ratio is gamma=βi/αi=1/r. Apply Lecture 3's exact product-sum solution. The denominator $1+\gamma+\cdots+\gamma^{M-1}$ is a geometric series: subtract gamma times the sum to obtain $(1-\gamma)S=1-\gamma^M$. Thus


$$
u_1=\frac{1-r^{-1}}{1-r^{-M}},\quad u_i=\frac{1-r^{-i}}{1-r^{-M}}\quad(r\ne1),
$$


with neutral limit ui=i/M. This is exact for this birth–death mechanism, not an exact diploid viability-selection WF formula. Fecundity selection, survival selection and death/birth ordering can produce different transitions.
Resolve the numerical population-size convention

The source table says N=100 and lists neutral probability 0.01. Those numbers imply **M=100 units**, whereas preceding equations sometimes use 2N copies. We explicitly use M=100 for reproducing the table's model, not N=100 diploid individuals.

| Relative fecundity r | Correct u1 at M=100 |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.500000 |
| 1.1 | 0.0909157 |
| 1.01 | 0.0157087 |
| 1 | 0.0100000 |
| 0.99 | 0.00583200 |
| 0.9 | 0.00000295134 |

Values r<1 are disadvantages, correcting the slide's “advantage” wording. Increasing fitness increases probability, not certainty; even a sizable benefit commonly disappears while rare. Use stable numerical limits near r=1, rather than evaluating a floating-point 0/0.
The WF diffusion approximation and the meaning of s

For a new beneficial B in an additive diploid model, here define wbb=1,wBb=1+s,wBB=1+2s: **s is the heterozygous advantage**, as Hahn p.133 specifies. For small |s| and large Ne, drift variance is p(1−p)/(2Ne) and deterministic drift in frequency is approximately sp(1−p). The backward fixation equation is


$$
0=sp(1-p)u'(p)+\frac{p(1-p)}{4N_e}u''(p).
$$


Dividing the interior equation gives u″+4Ne s u′=0; integrate the exponential and apply u(0)=0,u(1)=1:


$$
u(p)\approx\frac{1-e^{-4N_es p}}{1-e^{-4N_es}}.
$$


For a single new copy with census N=Ne, p=1/(2Ne), this becomes $(1-e^{-2s})/(1-e^{-4N_es})$. If s>0, |s|≪1 and Ne s≫1, the denominator is near one and numerator≈2s. At s→0 the ratio tends to p. If instead s_total is a homozygous benefit and dominance is 1/2, our s=s_total/2 and the large-population result is approximately s_total, not 2s_total. If census N differs from Ne, insert p=1/(2N) in the general formula; do not silently replace the initial frequency.
Effectively neutral mutations and biological modifiers

The scale Ne|s| compares selection with drift: values much less than one imply weak selective influence; values much greater than one allow selection to shape probabilities more strongly. It is a gradual regime comparison, not a sharp universal threshold. In a small population, even deleterious alleles can fix; in a large one, beneficial copies still have early stochastic loss.

The slides discuss size changes, structure, migration, recombination, linked deleterious alleles and survival versus fecundity. These modify establishment and fixation **within specified models**; their direction is not universally determined from a single word such as “structure”. Population decline can increase stochastic loss, migration can rescue or dilute an allele depending on source fitness/environment, and linked deleterious backgrounds can reduce establishment. Positive selection and a single-origin completed sweep are not synonymous: origins, standing variation and recombination determine genomic signatures, developed in Lecture 8.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. variables: $r$: relative haploid fecundity in the specified Moran mechanism; $M$: haploid units
$s$: heterozygous advantage in wbb=1,wBb=1+s,wBB=1+2s
$N$: census diploid individuals (sets new-copy frequency); $N_e$: effective drift scale
lessons.workedExample: WF approximation: Ne=N=10,000, heterozygous s=0.01 and p=1/20,000 give numerator $1-e^{-0.02}=0.0198013$, denominator $1-e^{-400}\approx1$, so u≈0.0198013, near 2s=0.02. Neutral chance is 0.00005: selection greatly improves probability, but about 98% of these new copies still do not fix. A mutation with the same homozygote advantage 0.01 and additive dominance has heterozygote advantage 0.005, giving approximately 0.01 instead. The exact Moran M=100,r=1.01 value 0.0157087 uses a different model and cannot be compared as if all parameters and clocks were identical.

lessons.moduleTitle: Lecture 6: Fate of mutations with selective effects
lessons.moduleDescription: Fitness, dominance, fixation probability, purifying selection, and mutation–selection balance.
lessons.title: Purifying selection and mutation–selection balance
lessons.summary: Balance recurrent mutation against genotype-specific removal and explain why harmful alleles can persist.
objectives: Derive exact recessive viability loss and approximate equilibrium
Derive the nonrecessive low-frequency balance with a specified dominance model
Interpret equilibrium assumptions and limitations from drift, mutation direction and linkage
sections: Two opposing fluxes

Let a be a deleterious allele introduced from A at forward mutation probability μ per copy per generation. With wAA=wAa=1,waa=1−sd, selection affects only recessive homozygotes. Before selection genotype contributions are p²,2pq,q². After weighting the contributions are p²,2pq,q²(1−sd); their sum is 1−sd q², so normalize by this mean fitness.

The a frequency immediately after selection is


$$
q_s=\frac{pq+q^2(1-s_d)}{1-s_dq^2}=\frac{q-s_dq^2}{1-s_dq^2}.
$$


Subtracting from q gives exact selective loss $q-q_s=s_dpq^2/(1-s_dq^2)$. The fitness cost does not act independently on every rare copy: most rare a alleles are in heterozygotes and hidden from recessive viability selection.
Derive the equilibrium rather than memorize it

Specify the order: selection then forward mutation. With no back mutation,


$$
q'=q_s+\mu(1-q_s).
$$


For small μ and rare q, ps≈p≈1 and sd q²≪1, selection loss≈sd q² while mutation input≈μ. Set the net change approximately zero:


$$
\mu-s_dq^2\approx0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\hat q\approx\sqrt{\mu/s_d}.
$$


This is a deterministic, low-frequency approximation, not an exact finite-population stationary frequency. Mutation may be per locus here; do not insert a genome-wide mutation probability into a single-locus formula. Genotype frequency of affected aa is approximately qhat² under the mating assumptions, distinct from carrier frequency 2pq.
When heterozygotes are selected

Hahn's discussion of dominance motivates a supplementary nonrecessive derivation. Let wAA=1,wAa=1−hsd,waa=1−sd. Mean fitness is $1-2hs_dpq-s_dq^2$ and


$$
\Delta q_{\rm sel}=-\frac{s_dpq[h+(1-2h)q]}{\bar w}.
$$


For q≪1 and h>0 with heterozygote removal dominating homozygote removal, this is approximately −hsd q. Balancing forward input μ gives


$$
\hat q\approx\frac\mu{hs_d}.
$$


The approximation also needs μ≪hsd and q small enough that the q-dependent term is negligible. Taking h→0 in this formula diverges rather than producing the recessive result; the dominant removal term changed, so use the square-root expression instead.
Persistence, drift and empirical inference

Finite populations fluctuate around deterministic expectations, sometimes lose the deleterious state and later reintroduce it by mutation. Strongly recessive alleles can persist at appreciable carrier frequency while homozygotes are rare. Back mutation, migration, changing environment, population structure, selfing and epistasis alter the balance; linkage to selected backgrounds changes establishment and local effective size.

A measured harmful allele does not prove adaptation, balancing selection or equilibrium. Its frequency can reflect mutation input, weak exposure in heterozygotes, recent demographic change or drift. Conversely, absence from a small sample does not prove complete evolutionary removal. Use genotype-specific functional/fitness evidence and population sampling before interpreting the persistence of a variant. The slides' later genomic signatures are taught in Lecture 8 so that deterministic fitness and statistical evidence are not confused.

variables: $q$: deleterious a frequency; $p=1-q$; $q_s$: after-selection frequency
$s_d>0$: recessive/homozygote relative loss; h: dominance of the harmful fitness effect
$\mu$: forward per-copy mutation probability at the modeled locus per generation
lessons.workedExample: Let μ=$10^{-6}$ and sd=0.01. Fully recessive balance predicts $\hat q=\sqrt{10^{-4}}=0.01$, aa frequency≈$10^{-4}$ and carriers≈$2(0.99)(0.01)=0.0198$. At q=0.01, exact selective loss is $0.01(0.99)(0.01)^2/(1-0.01(0.01)^2)=9.9000099\times10^{-7}$, close to mutation input. For h=0.5 at the same rates, nonrecessive qhat≈$10^{-6}/0.005=0.0002$, with aa≈$4\times10^{-8}$ and carriers≈0.00039992. Heterozygote exposure changes equilibrium dramatically without changing the mutation source.

lessons.moduleDescription: Site-frequency spectra, population-size change, model fitting, and uncertainty in demographic inference.
lessons.title: The site-frequency spectrum as demographic evidence
lessons.summary: Build single- and multi-population spectra and connect demographic parameters to genealogical and genomic predictions.
objectives: Construct folded/unfolded/joint spectra and calculate diversity from class counts
Predict demographic effects without assigning one unique cause to a spectrum
Compare SFS, HMM, ABC and haplotype inference families and define candidate-history parameters
sections: An alignment is reduced to counts

For n chromosomes, ξi counts sites with i derived copies. S=Σξi and locus pi=$\sum_i i(n-i)\xi_i/\binom n2$. A folded spectrum replaces i by min(i,n−i), preserving S and pi but losing ancestral/derived direction. SFS summaries discard exact nucleotide states, site positions and between-site associations; they retain counts and frequency weighting. This reduction helps fit large datasets but loses LD/haplotype information that might distinguish histories.

The current six-genome, 23-position slide example lists derived counts 4,3,1,2,1,1,2. These give ξ1=3,ξ2=2,ξ3=1,ξ4=1,ξ5=0; S=7. Folded counts are η1=3,η2=3,η3=1. Pi is $(3\times5+2\times8+1\times9+1\times8)/15=3.2$ differences per locus, or 3.2/23=0.139130 per site. Treat this short illustrative alignment as a teaching example, not a genome-wide diversity estimate.
Neutral expectations and demographic alternatives

Under a neutral constant-size panmictic infinite-sites model, E[ξi]=theta/i; Lecture 5 derives the genealogical connection. Growth often lengthens external branches relative to internal ones and creates an excess of recent rare variants. A bottleneck can remove rare alleles, shorten trees and transiently enrich intermediate variants; re-expansion generates new rare variation. The time of sampling after a bottleneck changes both amount and spectrum, so “bottleneck” does not have one permanent Tajima-D sign.

The Fogo spectrum prompts a hypothesis about history. Sweeps, purifying selection, structure, polarization errors and discovery filters can overlap demographic signatures. Outgroup choice determines unfolding reliability; ascertainment removes particular frequency classes. Use callable sites, invariant-site counts and sample design when comparing histories rather than normalizing away every absolute diversity difference.
Joint spectra: split versus migration

For populations with n1 and n2 chromosomes, ξij counts sites with i and j derived copies. Private polymorphism lies on edges where one count is zero; shared polymorphism occupies interior cells. Fixed differences and invariant corners are included or excluded according to the fitting scheme. Marginal spectra sum along axes, losing the cross-population pairing.

In the slide's split-time/migration gallery, recent divergence tends to preserve sharing; migration can also maintain sharing after older divergence. Inspect the full distribution, including private rare alleles and joint asymmetry, rather than identifying both histories from a diagonal alone. Human and Cape Verde examples illustrate why a recent split and high migration need explicit alternative models. Directional migration and unequal sampling sizes can change the two axes differently.
Four inference families and model parameters

SFS-based approaches such as fastsimcoal2 and dadi compare expected counts under candidate demographic histories; they commonly use a composite likelihood because linked sites are not independent. HMM/sequential-coalescent approaches such as PSMC and MSMC use information along chromosomes; genealogical tools such as Relate infer local ancestral relationships. Approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) compares simulated summary statistics to observed ones, retaining parameter values whose predictions match under a chosen tolerance. Haplotype-based approaches use shared tracts and associations, often informative about recent events.

A candidate history can include ancestral/reference size Nref, split time Tsplit, current descendant sizes, bottleneck size and time Tbot, exponential growth and separate m12,m21 migration rates. Specify forward migration direction: a backward lineage-migration probability generally also depends on relative sizes and is not the same raw parameter. Supplementary exponential growth can be written $N(t)=N_0e^{gt}$ for **forward** time t and growth rate g per generation; backward-time signs reverse. The next two lessons connect estimator contrasts, local coalescence and likelihood fitting rather than treating these tool names as interchangeable algorithms.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
variables: $n,n_1,n_2$: sampled chromosomes, not individuals; ξ and η denote unfolded/folded counts
$\theta$: matched locus mutation parameter; $T_{\rm split},T_{\rm bot}$: elapsed times in stated units
$m_{12},m_{21}$: directional migration parameters; define source/destination and time direction
lessons.workedExample: For an original joint-spectrum example, take four chromosomes in each population and observe ξ10=3,ξ01=2,ξ22=1,ξ31=1 (all other included polymorphic cells zero). The site ξ31 has minor count 1 in population 1 but is a **high-derived** variant there. Folding both axes would lose that distinction. Sharing alone is consistent with retained ancestral variation or migration; joint modeling is needed to distinguish their contributions.

practice.question: Why can two histories have the same marginal spectra but different joint spectra?
practice.solution: The same one-population counts can be paired at different sites across populations; the joint table retains that association.

practice.question: Explain one information loss caused by an SFS.
practice.solution: Discarding genomic order loses haplotype blocks and the spatial pattern of variants.

practice.question: Choose two demographic models for a rare-rich island spectrum.
practice.solution: Compare isolation with growth and isolation with a bottleneck followed by growth; examine joint data, LD and technical filters rather than declaring one history from rare counts.

lessons.title: Diversity contrasts and coalescent demographic histories
lessons.summary: Use diversity contrasts and local coalescence histories to interpret demographic evidence and its resolution limits.
objectives: Compute Tajima D on a consistent locus scale with explicit sample constants
Explain HMM emissions/transitions, coalescence hazards and relative CCR
Interpret haplotype resolution, geography, structure and smoothing as limitations
sections: Tajima D is a standardized contrast, not a selection coefficient

Pi and thetaW estimate the same neutral-equilibrium theta but weight variants differently. Define locus-level pi and S, then


$$
D=\frac{\pi-S/a_1}{\sqrt{e_1S+e_2S(S-1)}}.
$$


The denominator is a standard deviation, correcting the selection-slide's variance wording. For n chromosomes, the supplementary standard no-recombination constants are


$$
\begin{aligned}a_1&=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}1/i,&a_2&=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}1/i^2,\\b_1&=(n+1)/[3(n-1)],&b_2&=2(n^2+n+3)/[9n(n-1)],\\c_1&=b_1-1/a_1,&c_2&=b_2-(n+2)/(na_1)+a_2/a_1^2,\\e_1&=c_1/a_1,&e_2&=c_2/(a_1^2+a_2).\end{aligned}
$$


Here a1 is the earlier harmonic an, not a derived-count index. The constants arise from the neutral variances and covariance of the two estimators; they standardize sampling/evolutionary variability. Do not insert per-site pi in a numerator containing unnormalized S/a1. With no segregating sites, the standardized ratio is undefined; it is not a neutrality proof. Recombination, missingness and demographic models affect calibration, so D is not universally standard-normal.

Negative D indicates relatively many low-frequency variants; positive D relatively more intermediate-frequency variants. Growth, a sweep or purifying selection can give negative values; structure, contraction or old balancing selection can give positive ones. In Lecture 8 use genome context and calibrated nulls, not D sign alone.
Local genealogy is a hidden state along the genome

The sequentially Markovian coalescent approximates changes among genealogies at neighboring positions. In a PSMC-style HMM, the hidden state describes a discretized pair coalescence time; observed heterozygous and homozygous sequence patterns are emissions; recombination drives transitions among states. A low-mutation approximation to pair difference probability at a site with time T is $2\mu T$, or an at-least-one-event probability $1-e^{-2\mu T}$ before allowing finite-state/back-mutation complications.

PSMC uses information in a diploid genome's two homologs. MSMC incorporates multiple haplotypes and has different ancestral summaries; extra haplotypes improve resolution near the present. Phasing and error matter. Relate is a genealogy-based approach, not literally the same PSMC HMM; it is listed with coalescent genomic methods in the lecture, and its inferred trees support related demographic analyses. These methods exploit genomic order discarded by SFS summaries, while approximating the full ancestral recombination graph.
From coalescence hazard to size and cross-coalescence

In a panmictic diploid pair model, instantaneous hazard $\lambda(t)=1/[2N_e(t)]$ per generation yields


$$
P(T>t)=\exp\left[-\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du\right],\qquad N_e(t)=\frac1{2\lambda(t)}.
$$


Observed local genealogical histories inform these hazards, not a literal count of past individuals. For two populations the slide defines relative cross-coalescence


$$
\mathrm{CCR}(t)=\frac{2\lambda_{12}(t)}{\lambda_{11}(t)+\lambda_{22}(t)}.
$$


Rates between and within populations have matching inverse-time units. Before a split in a homogeneous common ancestor, relative CCR is about one; after complete isolation it tends toward zero. Migration, ancestral structure and unequal sizes complicate that interpretation. A smoothed crossing or midpoint is not an exact dated population split.
What the Arabidopsis case studies teach

The slides compare African and Eurasian ancestral-size curves, then eight-haplotype trajectories and high African Ne during pluvial intervals. Pluvial conditions can open Sahara dispersal corridors, but temporal correlation is not alone proof of a causal population expansion. Broader African sampling revises a formerly Eurasia-centered historical hypothesis; missing geographic populations can change inferred origins.

Population structure can make inverse coalescence-rate curves look like changing size even when local demes are constant. Instantaneous changes are smoothed by time bins and the inference method. Madeira bottleneck simulations spanning severity 0.1–1 in the slides support low long-term size without evidence for a particular colonization bottleneck in that analysis; failure to detect one is not proof none occurred. A ghost lineage can change the relationship between Morocco and Cape Verde. Treat fine case-panel dates as source-specific estimates with uncertainty, rather than an established universal origin story. These limitations connect directly to explicit model fitting in the next lesson.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
variables: $\pi,\hat\theta_W$: differences per locus; S: segregating sites; n: chromosomes
$e_1,e_2$: sample-size constants; D: dimensionless standardized contrast
$\lambda_{11},\lambda_{22},\lambda_{12}$: matching within/between coalescence hazards per generation; t: time backward
lessons.workedExample:
At n=10,S=20,pi=5 differences per locus, a1=2.82896825,a2=1.53976773. The constants give e1=0.019060534,e2=0.004948928. ThetaW=20/a1=7.069715; denominator=$\sqrt{0.019060534(20)+0.004948928(20)(19)}=1.503929$. Thus D=(5−7.069715)/1.503929=−1.376205. The sign shows a relative rare-variant excess; it does not identify growth versus selection or establish a calibrated significance level.

If coalescence rates within groups are 0.00005 and 0.00005 per generation and between-group rate is 0.00001, CCR=$2(0.00001)/(0.0001)=0.2$. A homogeneous pair hazard 0.00005 corresponds to Ne=10,000, but that inverse-rate interpretation requires the panmictic model.

practice.question: Would converting both theta estimates to per site change D if the entire variance were also rescaled consistently?
practice.solution: No: numerator and SD both divide by L. The error is mixing locus and site scales.

practice.question: Why do more haplotypes improve recent inference?
practice.solution: More recent lineages offer more recent coalescent events/information; additional data still require accurate phasing and modeling.

practice.question: How could structure mimic a population-size change?
practice.solution: Lineages can spend time in different demes before meeting; changing their meeting hazard changes inverse-rate size even without local-size change.

lessons.title: Demographic model fitting and uncertainty
lessons.summary: Fit demographic parameters with explicit likelihoods, compare candidate histories and report calibrated uncertainty.
objectives: Distinguish likelihood from probability and posterior inference
Derive composite SFS likelihood, Poisson mutation and branch-class probabilities
Compare histories with LRT/AIC and interpret island case studies with uncertainty
sections: Probability of data, likelihood of parameters

A parameter vector Θ may contain sizes, times, growth and migration. For observed data X, likelihood is $L(\Theta;X)=P(X\mid\Theta)$ treated as a function of Θ; it is not $P(\Theta\mid X)$. A Bayesian posterior also needs a prior and normalization. MLE is $\hat\Theta=\arg\max_\Theta L(\Theta;X)$, or equivalently the log likelihood.

The lecture regression analogy writes $y=X\beta+\beta_0+\epsilon$. To obtain an actual likelihood, specify an error distribution, such as independent normal residuals with variance σ². Here y is the observed response vector, X the design matrix, β slope coefficients and β0 intercept; the later population-genetic X denotes the genomic observations rather than that regression design matrix. The best fit is a candidate parameterization among models searched, not evidence the history is uniquely true.
Recover the image-only composite likelihood

For n chromosomes across L callable positions, let S be polymorphic sites, mi=ξi be SFS counts with Σmi=S, P0 probability of invariance, and pi the derived-count-i probability **conditional on a polymorphic site**. Then the slide's fastsimcoal form is


$$
L_c(\Theta;X)\propto P_0^{L-S}(1-P_0)^S\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}p_i^{m_i}.
$$


The omitted combinatorial factors depend on the observed counts and not Θ, so they do not change MLE for a fixed dataset. Taking logs gives $(L-S)\ln P_0+S\ln(1-P_0)+\sum_i m_i\ln p_i$. The three parts compare invariant-site fraction, mutation amount and frequency distribution. Across populations replace classes i with joint classes ij and their probabilities.

Linked sites are not independent observations. Multiplying their marginal probabilities produces a **composite** likelihood, not the full correlated-data likelihood. Its curvature can underestimate uncertainty; use appropriate block/bootstrap or calibrated composite-likelihood methods. Different filters, callable length or conditioning schemes require different likelihoods; never compare models fit to different observations by a naive AIC difference.
How genealogical simulations enter the probabilities

For total branch exposure B generations, mutation count K satisfies $P(K=k\mid B)=e^{-\mu B}(\mu B)^k/k!$ and $P_0(B)=e^{-\mu B}$. These are probability masses, not a continuous density. Across random genealogies, $P_0=E[e^{-\mu B}]$, generally not $e^{-\mu E[B]}$. The slide's t must represent branch exposure in that simplified expression, not merely the tree's chronological height.

Under a low-mutation single-hit approximation, a segregating event falls in frequency class i with probability proportional to the branch length Bi subtending i tips:


$$
p_i\approx\frac{E[B_i\mid\Theta]}{E[B\mid\Theta]},\qquad \hat p_i=\frac{\sum_{z=1}^Z B_{i,z}}{\sum_{z=1}^Z B_z}.
$$


This ratio of totals differs from averaging Bi,z/Bz; long trees supply more mutation opportunity. For simulated exposures B1=10,B2=30 with class-i exposures 5 and 3, the ratio is 8/40=0.2, whereas the unweighted mean of ratios is 0.3. Demographic parameters enter through these genealogy distributions; the source's wording “not a function of demographic parameters” must not be interpreted literally. Simulate enough genealogies and repeat optimization to manage Monte Carlo error and local maxima.
Model choice and uncertainty

For nested models and a valid full likelihood with regularity, the supplementary likelihood-ratio statistic is $2(\ell_{\rm full}-\ell_{\rm restricted})$, with an asymptotic chi-square reference based on extra identifiable parameters. Boundary parameters, nonidentifiability and composite likelihood require calibration rather than automatic chi-square use. Nestedness alone is insufficient.

The slide's AIC is $2k-2\hat\ell$, with k free parameters and maximized log likelihood ℓ. Lower values balance fit against complexity. Relative support is $e^{-(\mathrm{AIC}_i-\mathrm{AIC}_{\min})/2}$; dividing by the sum gives Akaike weights, not Bayesian posterior model probabilities. Composite AIC may need adjustment: the lecture table is a reported heuristic comparison, not a license to use uncorrected penalties for all correlated datasets.

Report parameter intervals, fit residuals, repeated fits and simulation-based predictive checks. Split time, size and migration can compensate for one another (identifiability). Mutation-rate and generation-time choices set absolute size/time scales. A better fit to a misspecified model need not recover real history.
Cape Verde: what the candidate comparisons establish

The island analysis compares simple split, exponential change, isolation-with-migration and bottleneck models, with reported AIC 784.3,635.0,620.0,573.8. The bottleneck candidate is best among those fitted: the migration model is 46.2 AIC units higher. Rounded log-likelihood values need not reproduce the last decimal of AIC exactly. Its fitted scenario gives island divergence near 3.7–4 thousand years, low local Ne (roughly 10³–10⁴), and a Fogo bottleneck near 0.93 thousand years in the illustrated model.

For Morocco versus the islands, the source compares simple split, exponential, isolation-with-migration, one-sided and two-sided bottlenecks. Reported AIC values are 928,758,2112,800,708; the two-sided bottleneck is the best reported candidate. The diagram places their split around 50 thousand years, with larger mainland ancestral/current sizes. A 50-thousand-year population split does **not** automatically date island colonization: unsampled “ghost” history and later movement can intervene. The lecture ends with that unresolved colonization question, appropriately preserved as uncertainty rather than answered by assumption.

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. variables: $L,S,m_i$: callable sites, polymorphic sites and SFS counts
$P_0$: invariant probability; $p_i$: conditional polymorphic class probability; $Z$: simulated genealogies
$\Theta$: demographic parameter vector; $k$: free parameters here (not lineages); $\ell$: log likelihood
lessons.workedExample: For an original three-chromosome dataset with L=100,S=4,m1=3,m2=1, and candidate P0=0.95,p1=0.75,p2=0.25, log composite likelihood excluding count-only constants is $96\ln0.95+4\ln0.05+3\ln0.75+\ln0.25=-19.156426$. If two candidates have maximized logs −120 with k=3 and −116 with k=6, their AIC values are 246 and 244. The latter improves fit enough to offset its parameter penalty. Relative support for the first versus second is e⁻¹=0.367879; normalized weights are about 0.26894 and 0.73106. Those values compare candidates on the same observations, not probabilities that either is literally true.

The bottleneck candidate is best among those fitted: the migration model is 46.2 AIC units higher. Rounded log-likelihood values need not reproduce the last decimal of AIC exactly. Its fitted scenario gives island divergence near 3.7–4 thousand years, low local Ne (roughly 10³–10⁴), and a Fogo bottleneck near 0.93 thousand years in the illustrated model.

For Morocco versus the islands, the source compares simple split, exponential, isolation-with-migration, one-sided and two-sided bottlenecks. Reported AIC values are 928,758,2112,800,708; the two-sided bottleneck is the best reported candidate. The diagram places their split around 50 thousand years, with larger mainland ancestral/current sizes. lessons.title: Selective sweeps and linked neutral variation
lessons.summary: Explain sweeps, balancing selection and background selection through linked neutral genealogies and their distinct statistical expectations.
objectives: Connect hitchhiking and recombination to local diversity and spectrum changes
Distinguish hard/soft/partial sweeps, balancing mechanisms and background selection
Evaluate Tajima D, high-derived variants and domestication bottleneck contrasts
sections: Genomic context and hitchhiking

A genome includes coding genes and surrounding regulatory, repetitive and other sequence. A neutral site can respond to selection elsewhere if inherited on the same chromosome background. During a beneficial allele's rise, linked neutral copies on its successful background also increase: genetic hitchhiking. In a simple single-origin hard sweep, lineages near the target trace to the successful ancestral background and recent coalescence reduces local variation.

Recombination can transfer a lineage out of that background; its chance depends on genetic rather than merely physical distance. A supplementary hazard approximation is


$$
P(\text{no escape})\approx\exp\left[-r\int_0^{T_s}(1-p(t))\,dt\right],
$$


where r is per-generation recombination fraction to the target, p(t) its frequency trajectory and Ts sweep duration. The complementary probability describes at least one escape under this simplified single-background model. Stronger/faster selection or lower recombination generally widens the linked effect, but no universal “s/r” number predicts every empirical window.
Sweep phase and origin matter

Before a sweep there is an older diverse genealogy; while the favored allele rises, its carriers share recent haplotype history; after fixation, new mutations rebuild variation on short branches. The selection deck emphasizes low diversity and rare new variants, often pi<thetaW and negative Tajima D. Recombinant flanks can also retain high-frequency derived variants, motivating thetaH and Fay–Wu H. A hard sweep is one successful origin; a soft sweep from standing variation or multiple origins can retain more haplotypes. A partial sweep has not fixed. These Hahn supplements explain why positive selection is broader than one textbook pattern.

Very near a completed target, S can approach zero and standardized spectrum statistics may be undefined or powerless. Recombination, elapsed time, background mutation and window size determine what remains detectable. Absence of a hard-sweep pattern does not exclude polygenic adaptation or an old selective event.
Balancing mechanisms produce different ancestry

Long-lived balanced allelic classes preserve deep internal branches and can elevate linked diversity and intermediate-frequency variants, giving positive D under suitable sampling. Self-incompatibility can favor rare recognition alleles; host–parasite cycles can make resistance benefit depend on pathogen prevalence; heterozygote advantage gives the stable interior equilibrium derived in Lecture 6. These mechanisms differ from a completed sweep, correcting the selection slide's copied “selective sweep” wording in its balancing explanation.

The A. lyrata defense-gene example compares D at candidate gene classes to the genome background. A higher distribution motivates old balanced polymorphism hypotheses but requires demographic/functional corroboration. Sampling only one allelic class or a young balancing allele can obscure the expected signature; a young balanced allele rising quickly can resemble an ongoing sweep.
Purifying linked selection and domestication

Background selection is loss of linked neutral copies when deleterious backgrounds are repeatedly removed. It often lowers local diversity, especially where recombination is limited, without requiring a beneficial fixation. Direct purifying selection at a focal coding site is distinct from its linked effect on nearby neutral sequence.

The ecological-genomics slides compare a genome-wide domestication bottleneck with additional diversity reduction at selected target genes. Founding drift affects much of the crop genome; a target-specific sweep can add a localized trough. Crop/wild diversity differences therefore require demographic and recombination-aware comparisons. The same statistical trough can reflect low mutation rate, background selection, a sweep or mapping error; do not treat every depleted region as an adaptation gene.

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
variables: $r$: recombination fraction per generation to the target; $T_s$: sweep duration in generations; p(t): target frequency
$\pi,\hat\theta_W,\hat\theta_H$: consistent locus-level diversity estimators
Fay–Wu H here is the unstandardized contrast; H is distinct from heterozygosity and a haplotype statistic

practice.question: Why can a sweep leave high-derived variants on its flanks?
practice.solution: Recombination can preserve old differences while successful backgrounds rise; their frequencies can be high relative to the outgroup.

practice.question: How does old balancing selection deepen a genealogy?

lessons.moduleDescription: Direct and linked signatures of selection, genome scans, and separation of selection from demography.
lessons.title: Genome-wide scans and empirical null distributions
lessons.summary: Move from statistical selection candidates to trait mapping and functional validation, with a fully derived QTL likelihood score.
objectives: Compare empirical/simulated scan nulls and account for linkage/multiple testing
Explain top-down and bottom-up gene discovery, QTL/GWAS/bulked segregants
Derive LOD from a fitted normal phenotype model and distinguish trait association from selected causality
sections: Outliers are candidates under a reference distribution

Genome scans compute window/locus summaries and compare them with an empirical genomic background or simulated demographic null. Tajima D contrasts pi and thetaW; FST compares population differentiation; Fay–Wu H uses polarized high-derived variation; direct dN/dS and polymorphism/divergence tests examine focal functional changes (T2). The selection deck's human chromosome-1 low-D regions and highland African maize SweeD examples motivate candidates, not conclusions from a single statistic.

SweeD is an SFS/composite-likelihood scan approach; accounting for a chosen demographic background does not make it universally “best”. Overlapping windows and LD mean several extreme SNPs may represent one event. Marker density, callable bases, map quality, mutation rate, local recombination and background selection can alter the baseline. A supplementary multiple-testing example: 1,000 calibrated tests at per-test 0.05 yield 50 false positives in expectation under an all-null set. Bonferroni controls family-wise error at α by threshold α/m; FDR procedures target the expected false-discovery proportion under their conditions. Linked tests still need valid marginal calibration and appropriate resampling; raw outlier ranks are not automatically P values.
Two discovery directions and the maize case

Top-down starts from a phenotype, uses QTL linkage or association mapping to locate regions, identifies candidate genes/variants, and tests population-genetic history. Bottom-up starts from a genomic selection signal, annotates candidates, then asks what trait and function were affected. Both need validation; an unusual sequence statistic is not a phenotype.

In the maize/teosinte branching illustration, parents differ, F1 progeny show some tillers and F2 segregate branching variation. Mapping recombination in a cross localizes a QTL; fine mapping and the teosinte branched 1 (tb1) gene/knockout comparison connect the interval to function. The genome-browser arrow identifies tb1, not every exact selected causal nucleotide. Its surrounding population-genetic pattern adds selection context but is distinct from the gene's effect on branching. We do not infer an unshown exact regulatory mutation from a map label.
Trait mapping: distinct designs, distinct assumptions

A QTL is a genomic region associated with quantitative trait variation in a defined design. Linkage mapping follows marker–phenotype cosegregation in crosses; GWAS compares population genotype–phenotype associations and must control ancestry/relatedness; bulked segregant analysis compares allele frequencies in pools at contrasting phenotype extremes. A signal interval can contain many linked variants and genes.

The amaranth seed-colour example combines GWAS, bulked segregants and QTL evidence for two regions across domesticates, with an MYB-like 1 candidate. Candidate orthology/function is suggestive, not a demonstrated causal mutation. Expression comparisons, random mutagenesis and targeted CRISPR perturbations provide different tests; use matched backgrounds and controls to separate causal effects from correlated expression or linkage. Nonmodel genomes and highly polygenic traits can make single-gene identification incomplete or misleading.
Recover and derive the image-only LOD appendix

At genomic position γ the slide defines


$$
\operatorname{LOD}(\gamma)=\log_{10}\frac{P(\boldsymbol y\mid\text{QTL at }\gamma,\hat\mu_{0\gamma},\hat\mu_{1\gamma},\hat\sigma_\gamma)}{P(\boldsymbol y\mid\text{no QTL},\hat\mu,\hat\sigma)}.
$$


The phenotype vector y has n measurements. Under the shown null, phenotypes are iid normal with common mean μ and variance σ²; a simple alternative uses two genotype-group means μ0γ,μ1γ and a common residual variance. Hats indicate maximum likelihood fits; γ is genomic position, not a mutation rate. Normal likelihood is $\prod_j(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\exp[-(y_j-\mu_{g_j})^2/(2\sigma^2)]$.

For an original known-group example, each mean's MLE is the group average and variance MLE is RSS/n. Substituting it into log likelihood gives $\hat\ell=-n[\ln(2\pi)+1+\ln(\mathrm{RSS}/n)]/2$. Common constants cancel, so


$$
\operatorname{LOD}=\frac n2\log_{10}(\mathrm{RSS}_0/\mathrm{RSS}_1).
$$


This reduction assumes the same observations and common homoskedastic normal residuals, with known genotype groups. Interval mapping with uncertain genotypes requires integrating group probabilities, not this unqualified simplification. LOD measures support for a QTL model, not probability that a gene is selected. Genome-wide scan thresholds require calibration (for example phenotype permutation respecting the design); LOD=3 is not universally a significance cutoff.
From calculation to scientific work

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
variables: $L_{\rm QTL},L_{\rm null}$: maximized phenotype likelihoods on the same data
$\gamma$: genomic map position; $\mu_{0\gamma},\mu_{1\gamma}$: genotype-group means; σ: residual SD
$n$: phenotyped individuals; RSS0,RSS1: sums of squared residuals; LOD uses base-10 logarithms
lessons.workedExample: Six original phenotype values are 0,1,2 for group 0 and 4,5,6 for group 1. Null common mean=3; RSS0=9+4+1+1+4+9=28. Alternative means=1,5; RSS1=1+0+1+1+0+1=4. Fitted residual variances are 28/6 and 4/6, respectively. Thus LOD=$3\log_{10}(28/4)=3\log_{10}7=2.535294$. Likelihood ratio is $10^{\rm LOD}=343$. The data favor the specified QTL phenotype model, but six measurements and a selected map position do not establish a genome-wide calibrated P value, a causal nucleotide or historical adaptation.

For an original known-group example, each mean's MLE is the group average and variance MLE is RSS/n. Substituting it into log likelihood gives $\hat\ell=-n[\ln(2\pi)+1+\ln(\mathrm{RSS}/n)]/2$. Common constants cancel, so


$$
\operatorname{LOD}=\frac n2\log_{10}(\mathrm{RSS}_0/\mathrm{RSS}_1).
$$


This reduction assumes the same observations and common homoskedastic normal residuals, with known genotype groups. Interval mapping with uncertain genotypes requires integrating group probabilities, not this unqualified simplification. LOD measures support for a QTL model, not probability that a gene is selected. Genome-wide scan thresholds require calibration (for example phenotype permutation respecting the design); LOD=3 is not universally a significance cutoff.

In the [Practical Laboratory](/workspace/practical), record the sampling unit, data filters, assumptions and each calculation. Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. These links lead to existing workspaces; they do not imply that an additional source worksheet has been supplied.
Worked example:
Six original phenotype values are 0,1,2 for group 0 and 4,5,6 for group 1. Null common mean=3; RSS0=9+4+1+1+4+9=28. Alternative means=1,5; RSS1=1+0+1+1+0+1=4. Fitted residual variances are 28/6 and 4/6, respectively. Thus LOD=$3\log_{10}(28/4)=3\log_{10}7=2.535294$. Likelihood ratio is $10^{\rm LOD}=343$. The data favor the specified QTL phenotype model, but six measurements and a selected map position do not establish a genome-wide calibrated P value, a causal nucleotide or historical adaptation.

lessons.title: Distinguishing selection from demographic history
lessons.summary: Integrate genomic candidates with demographic, ecological and experimental evidence for adaptation.
objectives: Explain genome/omics layers and sequencing choices in ecological studies
Distinguish local adaptation from a statistical sweep candidate
Use demographic nulls and the amaranth case to evaluate independent domestication and validation
sections: The genome and omics connect mechanism to ecology

Genomes contain genes, transposable elements (TEs), regulatory sequence and structural variation. The slide's circular view adds DNA methylation and open-chromatin tracks in seedling versus leaf: accessibility and epigenetic state can depend on tissue, so annotation is not equivalent to constitutive function. Genomics surveys DNA; transcriptomics RNA abundance; proteomics proteins; metabolomics metabolites. Omics means a broad complement or process measurement, not a guarantee of complete or causal knowledge.

Whole-genome resequencing compares individuals against an assembly to call variation. Genotyping assays selected markers and can introduce discovery bias. Third-generation long-read methods help resolve structural/repetitive variation and haplotypes, but coverage, error and assembly quality still matter. Many ecologically important species are nonmodels with less mature resources. A phenotype may arise from environmental regulation or many small-effect loci, so single-gene candidate scans do not exhaust adaptive mechanisms.
Ecological evidence: phenotype, environment and fitness

The peppered-moth illustration connects coloration and predation in polluted versus unpolluted backgrounds; it motivates differential fitness, not simply a change in a DNA statistic. Reciprocal transplant compares genotypes/populations in each environment, ideally randomized with appropriate replication and fitness measurements.

Evidence of local adaptation commonly compares **local versus foreign** performance within each site. “Home versus away” comparisons for one population can be confounded by site quality: every genotype might perform better at a benign site. Heritable trait differences, environmental exposure and fitness consequences should be distinguished from plastic responses. A sweep candidate needs this ecological and functional context before being described as an adaptation mechanism.
Condition the genomic null on history

Demographic history affects genealogies widely; locus-specific selection often adds a local deviation, but linked selection can be widespread and recombination makes the genome heterogeneous. The selection deck shows genome-wide negative D in A. thaliana and positive skew in an A. lyrata SP sample, interpreted in their studies through expansion/bottleneck history. Timing and sampling influence these patterns.

Fit histories to appropriately chosen data, simulate under parameter uncertainty and compare local summaries to matched genomic/technical expectations. Distribution-of-fitness-effects (DFE) models describe how many mutations have different effects; demography and selection may need joint inference. Functional annotation, replicated environmental association and perturbation can strengthen a candidate, but their errors may be correlated. Learning-based methods mentioned in the slides can use richer genomic patterns, yet require training simulations whose assumptions match the data; they do not eliminate confounding or establish causation automatically.
Amaranth: multiple lines of evidence, several uncertainties

The slides present nutritious annual C4 dicot grain amaranths cultivated for about 8,000 years, a roughly 500-Mb genome and a “diploid (16 chromosomes)” description. We retain that count as a source label without asserting whether it means n or 2n; the convention needs instructor verification. The study resequences 121 individuals across five crop/wild groups, allowing both demographic and scan comparisons.

A sweep-intersection plot shows limited sharing among grain domesticates. Together with population relationships it supports the presented hypothesis of three independent domestications involving A. cruentus, A. hypochondriacus and A. caudatus from A. hybridus; A. quitensis also appears in the sampled wild groups. Limited shared signals alone would not establish three origins: power, LD, demography, different targets and time since selection can affect intersection counts.

Wild samples have dark seeds and many crop samples white seeds, but the source plot also shows variation. Two trait regions and an MYB-like candidate connect phenotype mapping with the bottom-up history. Evaluate whether the same loci/alleles and mechanisms underlie each domestication, and use expression, mutagenesis or CRISPR with appropriate controls. A causal trait gene is not automatically the target responsible for every regional sweep signal.

Use the [Research Project Workspace](/workspace/project) to turn a prediction into a testable comparison; use the [Data Analysis Studio](/workspace/analysis) to inspect sensitivity and uncertainty. In the [Presentation Studio](/workspace/presentation), explain one quantitative result, its biological meaning and an alternative explanation. lessons.moduleTitle: Theory extension: Recombination and linkage disequilibrium
lessons.moduleDescription: A focused extension from Hahn on recombination, LD statistics, and the population recombination parameter.
lessons.title: Recombination, linkage disequilibrium, and the population recombination parameter
lessons.summary: Quantify haplotype associations, derive recombination decay and connect LD to genealogies, admixture and empirical rate estimation.
objectives: Calculate D, signed D-prime, r² and regional LD with admissible bounds
Derive deterministic decay and distinguish genetic map units from physical distance
Interpret rho, recombination lower bounds, inference methods and gene conversion
sections: Linkage, haplotypes and the biological question

A haplotype is the combination of alleles on one chromosome segment. Physical linkage concerns co-inheritance during meiosis; linkage disequilibrium (LD) is a nonrandom **population association** among alleles. Linked sites need not be in LD, and admixture/structure can create LD between chromosomes. Recombination reassorts existing variants, unlike mutation which generates new states.

For loci A/a and B/b, define frequencies xAB,xAb,xaB,xab summing to one. Marginal allele frequencies are pA=xAB+xAb,pB=xAB+xaB; qA=1−pA,qB=1−pB. Define $D=x_{AB}-p_Ap_B$ and expand the four frequencies:


$$
x_{AB}=p_Ap_B+D,\quad x_{Ab}=p_Aq_B-D,\quad x_{aB}=q_Ap_B-D,\quad x_{ab}=q_Aq_B+D.
$$


Positive D indicates enrichment of the named AB/ab arrangements (coupling under that labeling); negative D enriches Ab/aB (repulsion). Flipping one allele label flips D. Phasing matters: an AaBb diploid could carry AB/ab or Ab/aB; genotype information alone does not resolve it.
Bounds, D-prime and correlation

Requiring all four frequencies to be nonnegative yields $D_{\min}=-\min(p_Ap_B,q_Aq_B)$ and $D_{\max}=\min(p_Aq_B,q_Ap_B)$. Therefore raw D magnitudes cannot be compared without considering allele frequencies.

We use a **signed** convention:


$$
D'=\begin{cases}D/D_{\max},&D>0,\\D/|D_{\min}|,&D<0,\\0,&D=0.\end{cases}
$$


The positive denominator preserves sign and bounds D′ within −1 to 1. Hahn Eq.4.3's displayed negative-denominator branch yields a magnitude; the text discusses signed range and commonly reported absolute values. We state our normalization explicitly to avoid silently mixing signed and unsigned conventions.

Allelic correlation squared is


$$
r^2=\frac{D^2}{p_Aq_Ap_Bq_B}.
$$


It measures predictive association and ranges 0–1 for valid polymorphic haplotypes. Monomorphic margins make the denominator zero, so r² is undefined. |D′|=1 can occur with three haplotypes while r²<1; complete LD by a D′ convention need not mean perfect prediction. In small samples missing a rare fourth haplotype can artificially inflate |D′|. Pairwise Fisher tests assess independence with sampling assumptions; regional summaries need multiple-testing/LD context.
Recombination decay and map units

Let c be the per-generation recombination fraction between the two markers (the app's former r; use c here to distinguish it from r²). In an infinite random-mating population with no selection, migration or mutation affecting association, recombination transfers a fraction c of the excess haplotypes toward independence:


$$
x'_{AB}=x_{AB}-cD,\quad p_A'=p_A,\quad p_B'=p_B,\quad D_{t+1}=(1-c)D_t.
$$


Thus $D_t=D_0(1-c)^t$ and $t_{1/2}=\ln(1/2)/\ln(1-c)\approx\ln2/c$ for small c. Because margins are constant, r² decays as $(1-c)^{2t}$ times its initial value. Random drift creates new association, so this deterministic decay is not a finite-population equilibrium prediction.

Two-marker c lies between 0 and 0.5 under ordinary meiotic segregation; multiple crossovers can restore the parental arrangement, so c does not count every crossing event. Genetic distance d in Morgans counts crossover exposure; 1 cM=0.01 Morgan, and for small distances c≈d. As a labeled supplementary no-interference map model, Haldane gives $c=(1-e^{-2d})/2$, derived because an odd number of Poisson(d) crossovers changes marker phase. Physical bases convert through a recombination map, not a universal bases-to-cM constant.
What generates associations besides tight linkage?

Drift, founding events, structure, admixture, selection and sampling affect LD. For mixing fractions y and 1−y of two populations with no within-population LD, the additional association is


$$
D_{\rm mix}=y(1-y)(p_{A1}-p_{A2})(p_{B1}-p_{B2}).
$$


This follows expanding the pooled haplotype frequency minus the product of pooled margins; it can be nonzero for unlinked loci. With y=1/2, A frequencies 0.8/0.2 and B frequencies 0.7/0.3, Dmix=0.25(0.6)(0.4)=0.06.

Hahn's Drosophila versus human LD-block examples and the Medicago distance-decay curve show differences in recombination landscape and history. Regional mean $Z_{nS}=2\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}^2/[S(S-1)]$ averages pairwise squared correlations over S polymorphic sites; S<2 makes it undefined. For pair values 0.1,0.2,0.3 at three sites, ZnS=0.2. LD across physical distance is not the same exponential as decay across generations; maps, rates and allele frequencies matter. Unphased genotype associations, multiallelic markers and multilocus LD require extended measures, not blindly applying the biallelic haplotype formulas.
Rho, local genealogies and the limits of rate inversion

Hahn uses $\rho=4N_ec$ for diploid autosomal loci. If c is an interval recombination probability, rho describes that interval; if c is per-base initiation rate, rho is per-base and must be multiplied by the modeled interval length. Theta/rho=μ/c cancels Ne only when both estimators represent compatible neutral-equilibrium scales; nonequilibrium recovery and linked selection can spoil empirical ratio interpretation.

Backward recombination splits ancestry into segments; later coalescence joins lineages. The ancestral recombination graph (ARG) contains local trees, with neighboring positions correlated. Hahn's reference sampling relation gives expected recombination count $E[R]=\rho a_n$ under its specified neutral ancestral-sampling convention, not the count necessarily detectable from SNPs. Lack of a polymorphic marker can conceal events.

The classic equilibrium heuristic $E[r^2]\approx1/(1+\rho)$ ignores finite sampling and is inaccurate near rho=0. Hahn also presents the finite-sample/allele-filter approximation


$$
E[r^2]\approx\frac{10+\rho}{(2+\rho)(11+\rho)}\left[1+\frac{(3+\rho)(12+12\rho+\rho^2)}{n(2+\rho)(11+\rho)}\right].
$$


It applies under its neutral small/intermediate-rho conditions and exclusion of low-frequency alleles; it is not valid for arbitrarily large rho. At rho=0 and large n it gives 5/11, rather than one. The weak-association sample background can approach 1/n when loci are effectively unlinked. An LD measurement cannot uniquely identify Ne and c separately.

For an original check of the finite-sample LD approximation, choose n=50 and rho=10. The leading factor is $20/(12\times21)=0.0793651$; the correction factor is $1+13(232)/(50\times12\times21)=1.2393651$. Their product is 0.0983623. The simpler $1/(1+\rho)$ gives 0.0909091. This modest difference does not make either a universally valid empirical inversion; their sample/allele-filter and rate-regime conditions differ.
Detecting events and estimating rates

Under infinite sites without homoplasy, all four biallelic haplotypes at a marker pair require recombination in ancestry (the four-gamete test). Recurrent mutation can also make four haplotypes, while actual recombination can remain undetected. Rm counts a maximal set of nonoverlapping four-gamete intervals as a lower bound. With K unique haplotypes and S binary polymorphisms, each mutation can add at most one haplotype without recombination, motivating $R\ge\max(0,K-S-1)$; Rh combines stronger multilocus bounds. A lower bound is not an unbiased event count.

Moment estimators exploit variance among pairwise differences $V_k=\sum_{u<v}(k_{uv}-\pi)^2/\binom n2$. Likelihood methods use two-locus haplotype configurations, conditional haplotype probabilities or simulated summaries; pairwise composite likelihood avoids fitting a complete ARG but needs calibrated uncertainty. Hotspots, missingness, phasing and demography affect inferred rate maps. LD-based historical rates need not equal present pedigree/gamete rates.

Gene conversion copies a short tract nonreciprocally and can break short-range association without changing association of markers flanking both tract ends. Parameters include initiation rate g per site/generation, mean tract length q in bases and ratio g/c under a matched event-rate convention. A geometric tract model uses termination probability 1/q. Short tracts may be undetectable between sparse SNPs; biased conversion can also change allele frequencies. This differs from crossing over's long-range reassortment.
